#3300. Advanced Metrology for Defect Detection, Tool Health, and Semiconductor Yield Enhancement



In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

What You Will Learn:

  • How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processes
  • How baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affected
  • How in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structures
  • When offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign material
  • How correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projects
Register now for this free webinar!

#3299. Amazon Alternatives: 24 Places to Shop Online Other Than Amazon

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Rolling Stone may receive an affiliate commission.

We have Amazon to thank (or blame) for completely transforming the way we shop. The e-commerce giant’s virtually endless product selection, massive inventory, and ultra-fast delivery options have made everything from streaming movies to ordering groceries from Whole Foods as easy as clicking a button.

While Amazon excels in convenience and variety, that same abundance can be overwhelming. Sifting through dozens of near-identical products can lead to decision fatigue, leaving many consumers frustrated or simply burned out. That’s just one reason more customers are exploring alternatives to Amazon.

Some want to support smaller businesses and independent creators instead of contributing to the fortune of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, whose net worth reportedly exceeds $270 billion. Others have grown uneasy about the company’s business practices and environmental impact, prompting them to take their spending elsewhere.

Although Amazon has made efforts to promote small businesses on its platform, its market dominance still makes some shoppers hesitant. If you’re among those looking to support independent sellers and ethical brands, there are plenty of great options available.

Sites like Etsy let you buy directly from makers and designers, while platforms such as Uncommon Goods showcase work from independent artists on everything from gifts to home decor. Shopping for bigger-ticket items? There are several excellent Amazon alternatives that offer great deals, some even matching or beating Amazon.

Right now, we’re in the middle of Black Friday and Cyber Monday, two of the biggest shopping holidays of the year. While Amazon is offering plenty of exclusive deals on its website, shoppers looking for other places to browse will find a growing list of online retailers offering more curated, mindful, or ethical shopping experiences.

Many of these sites streamline your search by carefully selecting products, saving you from endless scrolling. Plus, eco-conscious and socially responsible shoppers will appreciate that several of these companies are certified B Corporations, meaning they meet rigorous standards for transparency, sustainability, and ethical business practices.

Keep reading for some of the best non-Amazon places to shop online, whether you’re hunting for handmade gifts, stylish essentials, or deals that don’t require a Prime membership.

And if you’re perusing any of these sites for holiday gifts, keep in mind that shipping deadlines are approaching faster than you might think. Hanukkah begins in just a few days, so you’ll want to start ordering now. Christmas Eve falls on Dec. 24, with many retailers’ holiday shipping cutoffs landing around Dec. 15.

Best for travel, outdoors, and sports apparel and accessories.

If you’re looking for clothing, footwear, outdoor gear, and sports equipment, the best Amazon alternative is REI. Founded as a consumer cooperative, REI has long been able to use its membership dues to fund projects that promote conservation, diversity, and equity. To this day, $5 from the purchase of every lifetime membership is donated to the REI Cooperative Action Fund, which supports organizations “working to improve the health and well-being of people and communities through time spent outside.”Of course, you don’t have to be a member anymore to shop the best REI deals online (though members do get additional perks and discounts). We’ve been shopping at REI for years to get hard-to-find products or trip-specific gear, and the site continues to grow with unique product offerings and new brands today. Right now, they’re offering up to 50% off on all clearance products. Start your search at REI.com.

Best for groceries, supplements, and snacks.

Certified B Corporation Thrive Market launched in 2014 with a cause-driven mission to offer organic and natural groceries and other sustainable products at affordable prices. The membership-based online grocer allows shoppers to save 25 to 50 percent on more than 6,000 products spanning healthy foods, meat, pantry staples, wine, bath and body products, beauty and skincare, baby care, supplements, and home goods.Membership plans start at $5 per month (based on an annual subscription price of $59.95), and you can shop by diet and lifestyle (vegan, vegetarian, non-GMO, keto, paleo, raw, and more) as well as by values such as non-toxic, Environmental Working Group-verified, certified organic, cruelty-free, and others. We love using Thrive Market to stock up on groceries and pantry items, household goods, and everyday essentials, and their meat and seafood selection is surprisingly fresh. We’ve also found some of our favorite snacks and (sort of) good-for-you sweets through their marketplace, which stocks unique items from around the world. The site also has hard-to-find organic and specialty brands, which you can’t get at the big-box chains or on Amazon. Start shopping at ThriveMarket.com. Thrive Market offers promo codes, discounts, and deals all the time, too. See the latest offers here.

Best for fast, same-day delivery on everything from restaurants to retail.

Amazon may be known for Prime and its promise of two-day shipping (or sometimes even faster), but when you need something today, DashPass, DoorDash’s membership program, is the service we always turn to. Starting at just $9.99 per month — with a discounted $4.99 student plan — DashPass unlocks $0 delivery fees on everything DoorDash has to offer, including restaurants, grocery stores, retail shops, florists, and local fan favorites.

We’ve been loyal DashPass members for the past five years, and we genuinely wouldn’t switch to another delivery platform. It’s saved us more times than we can count, whether packing for a last-minute vacation, scrambling to send a gift, stocking up on simple things like paper towels (mid-cleaning session), or simply ordering a Gatorade after a night out when walking across the street somehow felt like too much.

The convenience alone makes it worth the fee, which is lower than Prime, which costs $14.99 per month. Sign up today to take advantage of a 30-day free trial — just don’t be surprised if you end up keeping it long after it ends.

Yes, you can buy men’s clothing on Amazon, but instead of turning to off-brand names that will fall apart the first time you wash them, we suggest turning to a retailer we’ve known and trusted for decades: Men’s Wearhouse. The men’s shopping platform has everything you’ll need to stock up this fall and change out your seasonal wardrobe, from sweaters to suit sets and even scarves.

Best for pantry items and household goods.

Think of HiveBrands.com as your favorite general store or emporium, filled with unique snacks, drinks, health and beauty products, and household goods. Almost all of the options are sustainably made, ethically sourced, and from socially conscious companies. But they’re also just great products too — think organic nut butter and homemade sauces for the pantry, and clean soaps and lotions for your skincare routine. We’ve found super gentle and eco-friendly cleaning supplies and bug sprays, too.Everything ships in recyclable boxes printed with non-toxic ink and filled with 100% recyclable packing materials. Every order is carbon-neutral, too. What we like: Hive lets you shop by cause, whether you want to support brands helping small communities improve their livelihood, brands dedicated to championing equality, or female-owned businesses. You can shop by your preferred attributes too — like cruelty-free, Made in the USA, vegan-friendly, and more.

Sure, you can order fresh flowers with your Amazon Prime account for delivery, but we prefer to go through a site like 1-800-Flowers instead. The online retailer has been around since the eighties and is our go-to for everything from beautiful rose bouquets to gift baskets and table arrangements that can be sent directly to you.

The site even lets you shop by occasion, making it simple to browse everything from sympathy arrangements to celebratory bunches. Depending on where you live in the United States, 1-800-Flowers offers same-day delivery (which often beats even Amazon’s fastest shipping option). You never have to worry about missing a birthday, graduation, or housewarming again — well, at least when it comes to flowers. You’ll still have to remember to RSVP.

Readers flock to Amazon every day to snag the latest novel they’ve been eyeing or the book everyone seems to be talking about after it was turned into a feature film. But here’s a trick: You don’t have to turn to the massive conglomerate to get the newest titles. You can find just as good — if not better — editions through Bookshop.

When you shop this way, you’re not sending more money to a billionaire who already has more than $270 billion. Instead, you’re supporting independent bookstores, because with each purchase, 30% of the sale goes to a smaller seller of your choice, according to the site.

Best for health/personal care products and cleaning supplies.

If you’re looking for a one-stop eco-conscious shop for non-toxic and cruelty-free household supplies, beauty and skincare, personal care, and wellness products, and also want to save yourself from the hassle of last-minute restocks, then you’ll want to try Grove. The online subscription service offers everything from dishwasher and bathroom soap refills to medicine cabinet essentials and compostable plastic bags (and much more) from popular brands such as Dr. Bronner’s, Seventh Generation, Method, Mrs. Meyer’s Clean Day, Tom’s of Maine, and others, alongside independent names.It works like this: You’ll add product subscriptions that you can customize by frequency — say, you need dish soap and sponges every month and laundry detergent every three months. So long as your order meets the minimum of $29, you’ll get all of your must-haves in regular deliveries, efficiently packed in recyclable materials. Oh, and it’s a B Corp., too. Start shopping at Grove.co.

Best for sending gift baskets, special treats, and flowers.

Harry & David is our top pick for special occasions, offering a wide selection of gift baskets, flowers, wine, and sweet treats. The brand ships nationwide, and they also provide expedited shipping if you’re on a tight schedule or working with a deadline.

Best for original online jewelry gifts and buying conflict-free diamonds.

If you’re in the market for a jewelry gift, one place we recommend looking is Blue Nile. Founded in 1999, the brand is the original online jewelry retailer and still one of the most trusted sources for diamond jewelry. The retailer sources conflict-free diamonds and offers education services for choosing the right pieces. They’ve since expanded to other types of jewelry, but diamonds remain their bread and butter. Plus, Blue Nile has impeccable customer service, ensuring that the ordering and any follow-up processes are painless.

We’re not alone in our appreciation for Blue Nile. Helen Mirren, Brooklyn Decker, Grimm star Bitsie Tulloch, and Giuliana Rancic are just a few celebrities who have been spotted wearing Blue Nile jewelry on red carpets.

Best for designer apparel and everyday essentials.

From designer apparel to everyday essentials, Nordstrom’s markdowns give shoppers the chance to invest in pieces that last, often with free shipping and easy returns, making the experience stress-free.

What makes Nordstrom’s website even more tempting is the selection of brands on sale. You can score deals on favorites like On Running, Nike, Rag & Bone, plus home essentials from Voluspa candles and Calvin Klein bed sheets. Whether you’re updating your sneaker rotation, refreshing your wardrobe, or stocking up on skincare, Nordstrom’s curated deals make it easy to shop for quality brands.

Best for workout (and athleisure) apparel, accessories, and footwear.

Training for a marathon? Heading to a new workout class? Lululemon has an incredibly versatile selection of everything from top-tier running shorts made for performance to bright tanks and tees that will have you standing out in a sea of neutrals. Over the last few years, Lululemon has worked to expand beyond the yoga studio (especially in the men’s department) with high-performance workout gear and ultra-comfy everyday clothing, and their styles frequently go viral for a reason. Instead of picking up cheap bike shorts that’ll ride up or pill immediately, this is a great place to shop for quality fitness gear that will last you through every workout (and every season).

Best for clothing, accessories, fitness equipment, and hiking equipment.

One of our favorite Amazon alternatives to shop these days is Huckberry.com. Once best known as an outdoor site, Huckberry’s online inventory now includes footwear, clothing, grooming, workout equipment, and even home decor. The site is pioneering what they call the “Everyday Adventure” category, which “sits between the traditional outdoor and fashion industries” while combining “the best of retail, media, and community.” The best part is that Huckberry offers a number of brands that you can’t find on Amazon, including new and emerging American designers. Their prices (and deals) are often pretty competitive too.

Sure, you can order ground or whole coffee beans on Amazon, but what you should really be turning to is Trade Coffee. Trade is a subscription-based service designed to cater to your individual tastes, helping match you with coffee that fits your preferences. It’s affordable, customized, and supports smaller businesses, so you can feel good about what’s in your cup with every sip.

Best for home goods, skincare, and bath and beauty.

We first discovered Public Goods during the pandemic when we stocked up on the site’s super-gentle soaps and hand sanitizers for our home. Since then, we’ve become big fans of the eco-friendly company’s Costco-meets-direct-to-consumer model. For an annual membership fee of $49, you’ll have access to the startup’s line of sustainable essentials, such as grocery staples and canned sundries, home cleaning products, personal care items (like bamboo toothbrushes and haircare), vitamins, pet food, and even CBD oils. While you don’t need to be a member to shop the site, members get lower prices, occasional deals, and freebies (sign up now and get $60 worth of goods and promos).The company touts transparency and ethically sourced ingredients among its values, and it’s able to pass along savings to its members by manufacturing its own products. You can shop by categories such as gluten-free, vegan, tree-free, and organic, and Public Goods works with nonprofit Eden Reforestation Projects to offset its carbon footprint by planting a tree for every order placed.

One of the biggest perks of ordering through Amazon Prime is the lightning-fast shipping — you can get whatever you need, from clothing to sleep aids like melatonin to last-minute accessories before an upcoming event or concert, delivered in less than two days.

So if you’re in that same kind of rush and need something ASAP, we turn to Revolve. The online retailer offers the latest in fashion, popular viral products, beauty, and accessories, with shipping speeds that rival Prime. They offer several delivery options, including next day by 12 PM, next day by 8 PM, and 2nd Day Air, in addition to standard free shipping within 3–5 business days.

In our experience, they’ve never let us down when we’ve needed something in a pinch. Between the impressive product selection and expedited delivery options, Revolve is our go-to when we need an order fast.

Best for fashion, home essentials, and toys.

Macy’s has long been a favorite of ours for just about… anything. The major retailer, which was first established in 1858, offers an extensive lineup of fashion, beauty, personal care products, home goods, décor, and more. What we like most is the fast shipping; many items can be delivered in just a few days, along with consistent sales and exclusive perks through its VIP membership program.

One standout feature we especially love: In 2021, Macy’s partnered with WHP Global to bring back Toys “R” Us, the nostalgic, once-beloved toy retailer, both online and in select brick-and-mortar locations. On Macy’s site, you can find all the classic offerings, from Barbie and LEGO sets to games and puzzles, in a dedicated section that keeps the brand’s iconic rainbow aesthetic alive. There are even some toys created exclusively for Macy’s, per the brand’s site.

It captures the same fun, variety, and affordable pricing that made Toys “R” Us so popular in the early 2000s. Only now, you can add it all to your cart from the comfort of home.

If you’re looking to add globally-inspired flavors or flair to your cooking or home decor, World Market (or Cost Plus World Market) is our go-to for fair-trade products that meet sustainability and ethical standards. The San Francisco-founded retailer stocks gourmet groceries, fair-trade coffee and teas, international pantry essentials, handwoven baskets, kitchen accessories, vintage-inspired home furnishings, and more from every corner of the world.We’ve picked up everything from lamps and pillows to chocolates and flowers from the store, which has an eclectic array of offerings. It’s a great place to shop for unique gifts, too, if you want an Amazon alternative.Can’t wait for your delivery, but need the convenience of online shopping? You can opt for same-day Curbside Pickup at your local store and score an additional 15% off when you join the company’s free membership program. Start shopping at WorldMarket.com.

Best for pet food, toys, and accessories.

What began as founder Dave Bolotsky’s virtual handmade marketplace has grown into one of the best places for shopping for handmade and one-of-a-kind gifts. Go to Uncommon Goods if you’re looking for cool finds by independent brands, designers, and makers. They’ve got everything from stylish jewelry and clothing to gourmet condiments and kitchen accessories to puzzles and home decor. This is our go-to site for unique gifts for birthdays, holidays, weddings, graduations, and more. We’ve purchased a lot of personalized gifts from Uncommon Goods, from wall art to toys to desk accessories.Vegans will be happy to know that the ethical online retailer only stocks leather-, feather-, and fur-free products. Many of their products are made from recyclable materials and packaging.The B corporation also donates $1 from every purchase to a nonprofit partner, uses eco-friendly packaging, pays its employees more than double the federal minimum wage, and advocates for paid family leave and better pay in the state of New York. Now, what’s a better Amazon alternative than that? Start shopping at UncommonGoods.com.

Best for getting freshly baked goods delivered to your door.

Amazon Fresh offers a wide selection of baked goods, from breads and pastries to other doughy favorites — but there’s another company giving it serious competition: Wildgrain. Founded in 2020, Wildgrain is a subscription-based service that, according to the brand, “delivers artisan breads, pastas, and pastries straight to your door”. The process is simple: You choose when your box arrives, what’s inside — including vegetarian or gluten-free options — and your preferred price range. Boxes start at just $69 and cap at around $189.

With hundreds of five-star reviews, Wildgrain is praised for its convenience and simplicity. Every item is made with good-for-you ingredients, giving you that fresh-from-the-bakery taste without ever leaving home. Get started here.

Best for crafts, decor, gift ideas, and DIY designs.

From fan-made merch to home decor and accessories, Etsy features thousands of sellers offering unique, often handmade goods for purchase. Once known as a destination for DIY crafters, Etsy is now a full-service marketplace that sells everything from vintage clothing and antiques to jewelry, tableware, and furniture. Etsy is one of our go-to destinations for gifting, with one-of-a-kind picks for Halloween, housewarmings, and the holidays alike. Unlike Amazon, there’s no Etsy warehouse — only a network of artisans and local sellers who sell and ship their goods directly to you. Start shopping here.

Amazon Fresh has made it easy to get groceries delivered to your door, but you can do the same thing with Instacart. The site and app offer a wider range of offerings than Amazon Fresh, with the same super-fast delivery times.Instacart offers same-day delivery from almost 600 national and local retailers, like Sprouts Farmers Market, ALDI, Costco, Publix, Wegmans, Jewel-Osco, Shaw’s, The Fresh Market, Fresh Thyme Market, and more. And it’s not just food and drinks either — Instacart can now deliver flowers, home accessories, and even beauty products from Sephora in as fast as an hour.Instacart is free to sign up for, though you’ll want to grab an Instacart Express membership to get free delivery (otherwise, delivery fees range from $1.99 to $9.99 in our experience). Right now, you can sign up for an Instacart Express free trial here to test out the service for yourself.

No list of the best alternatives to Amazon would be complete without mentioning Walmart. This mega discount superstore could be considered the original Amazon, as it offers daily competitive deals on a wide range of goods, from pantry products to clothing items and even pharmacy delivery. Walmart truly has everything you could possibly need, all in one place.

Additionally, Walmart has a membership program called Walmart+, which provides exclusive access to members-only sales, free delivery options, discounted streaming services (including your choice of Peacock or Paramount+), and special deals on partnered brands, from restaurant chains to other online stores. Walmart+ is available for $12.95 per month, but you can currently sign up for a 30-day free trial.

It’s hard to beat the Big Red Bullseye’s ridiculously convenient shopping options, especially on days like Prime Day, where Target often offers the same, if not lower, prices than Amazon. Target makes it easy to place an online order for deodorant, groceries, and bath towels and pick up your goods in-store or via its Drive Up option (simply wait in your car, and store staff will bring your purchases to you), or get everything delivered using Shipt’s same-day service.On top of its vast inventory, the mass retailer also offers a 5% discount whenever you use its RedCard debit or credit card. Don’t forget the retail giant’s smartphone app, which also boasts additional Target Circle deals. Is it as niche or as small a business to support like some of the other sites on our list? No. But does it deliver a ton of deals and exclusives that make it a worthy Amazon competitor? One hundred percent. Start shopping at Target.com.

How you feel about Amazon may also be the same way you feel about Temu, the Chinese e-tailer that offers millions of discount items for home and travel. Where else can you get $3 headphones or a $30 pizza oven? Like Amazon, Temu has millions of items in stock, from electronics to clothing to household essentials. Most of their items are made in China and are noticeably cheaper than those on Amazon, though shipping may take a few extra days if the products are coming from overseas. In our experience, you also get what you pay for. But if you need something in bulk or just want to test out a trend or viral product before committing to the real thing, Temu could be a good option for you.Of course, you’ll want to read up on Temu’s business practices before you decide whether or not you want to spend your money there. Congressional lawmakers have cited Temu’s sale of knockoff designer items and have asked the company for increased safety and compliance controls. A potential bright spot? Temu talks up its tree planting program, which partners with Trees for the Future to plant trees across Africa to benefit farmers in this region. Learn more here.

Tim Chan is the VP of Commerce at Penske Media, overseeing fashion, tech, lifestyle, and streaming coverage across marquee brands like Rolling Stone, Billboard, The Hollywood Reporter, Variety, and WWD, among others. Previously, Chan was the first-ever Lifestyle Editor at Rolling Stone, covering all things fashion, culture, and travel through an entertainment lens. #3298. This iPad Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off During Black Friday

If you're shopping for an iPad this holiday season, you might be a bit intimidated by Apple's price tags. The iPad mini starts at $599; the base iPad Air is $749; and the entry-level iPad Pro is a whopping $1,199. Most of Apple's iPad line certainly lives up to its expensive reputation.

That's where the iPad A16 comes in. This is Apple's least expensive tablet, with an MSRP of $449. But despite being Apple's "budget" option, the iPad A16 shouldn't be ignored by customers looking for the best all-around device. In fact, it's really the best iPad for most people, which is why I named it the best tablet gift of 2026. What's more, retailers are giving the iPad A16 a $50 discount ahead of Black Friday, bringing the entry-level price down to $399.

The iPad A16 isn't Apple's best iPad (that would be the iPad Pro). It doesn't have the best display, the best camera, or the best processor. But it doesn't need those things: This iPad has a display, camera, and processor that are good enough for most use cases, without unnecessarily driving up the price. Simply put, it's one of the best tablets you can buy right now.

The iPad A16 has a large, 11-inch (technically 10.86 inches, according to Apple's fine print) IPS display with a brightness of 500 nits. As the name implies, it has Apple's A16 chip, the same processor as the iPhone 14 Pro and iPhone 15. That chip is about four years old at this point, and while that means it won't be as fast as Apple's newer SoCs, it still holds its own with iOS 27. It comes with two cameras: One 12MP wide camera on the back, with support for 4K video recording, and a 12MP Center Stage camera on the front.

Apple says this iPad can run for 10 hours while browsing the internet on wifi or watching video. You charge the tablet with USB-C, which supports data transfer up to USB 2.0 (which nets you 480Mb/s transfer speeds). It also comes with other perks you might expect from Apple's more "pro" tablets. You can connect the iPad to an external display, up to 4K resolution at 60Hz. It also supports two Apple Pencil models: The USB-C Apple Pencil and the first-gen Apple Pencil.

The only real consideration here is storage: This model comes with 128GB of storage, which can run out fast. It's particularly usable for users who rely on cloud storage or mostly stream their entertainment. But if your giftee plans to store photos, videos, or music on their iPad, it's worth considering upgrading. The $50 discount applies to most storage models, as well as the cellular iPad options, except for the 512GB models: The wifi-only model has a smaller discount, while the cellular option has a $100 discount.

Sure, the iPad A16 doesn't have the fastest processor, an OLED display, support for newer accessories, or Apple's sharpest cameras. But all of the specs it does have are enough to run the things you need on iPadOS. If someone on your list is looking for an iPad for web browsing, streaming, messaging, and light gaming—and they don't need something for professional work—this device is likely more than enough iPad for them.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Yes, Apple participates in Cyber Monday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy, Amazon, and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

#3295. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok

The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Long-Distance Surgeon.”

Max G. Levy is an independent science journalist based in Los Angeles. His work has appeared in Wired, Quanta Magazine, and MIT Technology Review.

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Rolling Stone may receive an affiliate commission.

Skincare is far from just a trending topic on your TikTok or Instagram feeds; it’s a billion-dollar industry. From facial cleansers to cosmetic treatments and procedures, such as Botox injections, there are seemingly endless routes to the same thing: Clear and young-looking skin. That’s not even including apps like Facetune and various filters we can apply to our photos to hide even the suggestion of aging. In our society, getting older is taboo; something we may silently acknowledge as inevitable yet not really discuss, all the while doing anything and everything to “prevent” it from happening at all.

The truth is, there is no magic cure for aging. Try as you might, even the most knowledgeable skincare experts have yet to come up with a way to keep time from marching across our faces. That said, that doesn’t mean you can’t age gracefully, or that you have to completely empty your wallet to do so. By taking proper steps to care for your skin, you can not only ensure that it remains healthy throughout your life, but also slow down the effects of aging. One method is showing promising results: red light therapy.

Red light therapy has been clinically studied and shown to improve your skin’s overall appearance, helping combat wrinkles, scars, acne, and other signs of aging. To understand how it works, we must first understand why things like wrinkles appear in the first place.

“As we age, our cells become larger. This makes it harder for them to divide and multiply, which slows our bodies’ ability to regenerate,” says Shane Miller, a licensed esthetician and the owner of the popular Instagram account @howtohydrate.

That’s where red light therapy devices come in; these devices come in different forms, sometimes as masks you can wear on your face, and other times as panels you can hang and stand in front of. These red light panels administer low-wavelength red light to stimulate our skin cells, giving them the energy they need to continue the upkeep of our skin’s appearance and texture.

Regularly using red light therapy panels in moderation may help maintain a healthy sheen and improve any fine lines or wrinkles, as well as reduce inflammation that may appear as a result of conditions such as psoriasis, eczema, and contact dermatitis.

Miller recommends using your red light therapy device daily on a freshly cleaned and dry face, before you’ve applied any serums, moisturizers, and/or sunscreen if you’re using it during the day. Unlike UVA/UVB rays, red light does not pose a threat to your skin. However, it’s always a good idea to proceed with caution when introducing a new step into your routine, as everyone’s skin is different. Be sure to consult the instructions on any device, protect your eyes, and consult a dermatologist before use if you have any light sensitivities.

If you’re unsure of how to integrate red light therapy into your daily routine, Miller recommends consulting with a licensed esthetician or a dermatologist to see if it’s right for you.

We’ve rounded up some of the best red light therapy panels that you can buy online right now. Whether for your morning wake-up routine or for a post-work (or post-workout) recovery, all of these red light panels set up easily to help you rest and rejuvenate from the comforts of home.

If you want to experience the best possible red light therapy, check out this Helio Nova from Heliocure. The premium full-body panel offers the industry’s highest LED density (up to 1064nm wavelength), which translates to the best deep tissue penetration possible — and the best chance of real, noticeable benefits. The wavelength is adjustable between six settings, letting you target different benefits. Thanks to its size (65 inches tall), you won’t need to reposition during sessions, and it can be tilted to use horizontally.

Simple, straightforward, and effective, the Hooga red light panel makes rejuvenating your skin cells a breeze with 60 LED lights, user-friendly digital controls, and a built-in timer. Built-in cooling fans ensure that the panel is never too hot to the touch, while Hooga says its 60-degree beam angle perfectly directs the red light to your face and body.Hang this panel on a door hook or mount it on the included stand. This set includes protective goggles to keep your eyes safe during your session.

We use it for about ten minutes a day, and it’s been a game changer. Reviewers online agree, with Amazon shoppers giving this a 4.5-star rating (out of five) from hundreds of verified reviews.

A quick tip? When shopping for one of the best red light therapy panels on the market, look for one that’s backed by clinicians. Best of all, you don’t have to choose between one or the other; combine the two with the third setting to receive the best of both worlds.At 40.5 inches in height and designed with 200 LED bulbs, this is one of the most wide-reaching devices on our list. As you’re searching for your potential red light therapy panel, here’s what you should keep in mind.

Power: A panel with more power often means it’s more effective at energizing your cells. You might think wattage dictates power, but the truth is that wattage refers to how much energy is being consumed by the device. Instead, find out its irradiance, measured in milliwatts per square centimeter.

Size: This will dictate how much of your skin you’ll be able to treat in a session. A larger panel will be able to cover more skin.

Extra Features: Digital displays, self-timers, and fans are just a few examples of some additional features these devices can come equipped with. What else can your red light therapy panel do?

We chose our list of best red light therapy panels based on ease of setup, ease of use, and overall results. We also personally tested and used many of the devices on this list. Keep in mind: skincare and wellness results will vary from person to person. But in our testing, these were the best red light therapy panels for helping to boost energy, improving our skin texture, and helping with relaxation and recovery.

#3289. Understand How Satellite Links Shape IoT Device Design and Testing

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

In line with the company’s design language, these headphones feature transparent elements and bold, geometric detailing that make them stand out from typical matte-black pairs. But the appeal goes beyond the look. These IP52-rated headphones use 40mm drivers, hybrid ANC, and both USB-C and 3.5mm connectivity. They also support high-res audio via LDAC, while Nothing’s companion app gives you basic and advanced EQ controls for adjusting the sound. Battery life is impressive, too, stretching to 35 hours with ANC on and up to 80 hours with it switched off.

But the hardware alone doesn’t define the experience—Nothing’s control scheme is what makes these wireless headphones stand out. Instead of touch panels or clunky buttons, you get a satisfying volume scroll wheel (they call it the Roller), a multi-function Paddle for track navigation, and a customizable button that can switch EQ profiles or noise modes. WhatsApp just announced that it is rolling out scheduled messages, which it says is one of users’ most requested features. Here are the details.

From WhatsApp’s blog post announcing support for scheduled messages:

You can write a message when you think of it and send it anywhere from 10 minutes to 14 days later, in both your 1:1 and group chats.

To schedule a message, press and hold the send button and pick the date and time you want it to arrive. It will look like any other message to the person receiving it. You can see all future messages you have lined up, and delete them beforehand if you change your mind.

If you follow Apple closely, the company’s software release patterns quickly become clear.

For example, iOS 27.2 launched late last month around the same time as releases in years past. The only difference is that normally iOS 27.1 would launch in late October rather than 27.2. But since Apple made iOS 27.1 exclusive to iPhone Duo, all software releases for the iOS 27 cycle will be off by one number—despite following the same timing as ever.

That means iOS 27.3 is up next, and its release should align with historic patterns for x.2 updates.

Apple has confirmed that iOS 27.3 will launch to all users in December once beta testing concludes.

To get more precise though, here’s a sampling of release patterns for comparable x.2 updates the last few years:

Based on this pattern, iOS 27.3 is expected to release by mid-December.

Apple always tries to ship its last software update of the year with a little buffer before taking a holiday break. That way if any major issues arise, the company can develop a quick fix and push it out before much of the company takes time off.

Expect to see iOS 27.3 launch as early as the week of December 7, or on Monday, December 14 at the latest.

The Beckham Stack pairs two products. Daily Ultimate Essentials Pro packs 90+ ingredients across 16 supplement categories, and Daily Ultimate Longevity adds 10 compounds for long-term cellular health, including 600 mg of NMN.

Together, they cover what a demanding schedule wears down. Bose positions it right in the middle of the SoundLink lineup, and you feel that balance in how it’s built. #3280. Report: Apple gains ground as Latin American smartphone shipments plunge 24% in Q3

According to a new Counterpoint Research report, Apple increased its share of Latin America’s smartphone shipments in Q3 2026, recording the smallest decline among the region’s top five brands. Here are the details.

In a report released this week, Counterpoint Research says the ongoing memory crunch led to a 24% year-over-year drop in smartphone shipments during Q3, “the second-lowest quarter since 2015.”

Per the report, Samsung maintained its lead with a 35% shipment share, despite a 15% year-over-year decline in total shipments, well ahead of second-place Motorola, which captured 18% of shipments after a 23% drop. Interestingly, Motorola’s share actually increased one percentage point from a year earlier.

Rounding out the top five were Xiaomi, with a 14% share and a whopping 34% decline, Apple, with a 9% share and a 10% decline, and Honor, with an 8% share and a 27% decline.

Despite the decline in overall shipments, Apple’s shipment share increased by 2 percentage points from 7% a year earlier, moving the company from fifth to fourth place in the region.

Other brands collectively accounted for 16% of shipments, down from 19% a year earlier, with their combined shipments falling 37% year over year.

Here’s Counterpoint on Apple’s performance for Q3 in Latin America:

Apple was the most resilient, with the smallest decline among the top five brands (shipments down 10% YoY), and rose one position to No. 4 in the region. Apple absorbed the impact of price increases better than its rivals, helped by strong product availability. Apple launched the iPhone 18 Pro series at the end of the quarter. For the first time, Chile joined Brazil and Mexico in the first launch wave.

As for regional factors that contributed to the decline, Senior Analyst Benjamin Corona noted that Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia faced additional challenges beyond the global memory shortage, ranging from political uncertainty to inflation and tighter household budgets. Smartphone shipments fell 22%, 26%, and 28% in those countries, respectively.

Looking ahead, Counterpoint says it “expects the decline to ease in Q4 2026 as prices stabilize and seasonal demand returns,” adding that “memory-related price pressure should moderate by Q2 2027, but supply constraints will likely continue through the end of 2027.”

I give away a lot of keyboards. Sounds weird, I know, but stay with me here. I've reviewed dozens of keyboards. I once had a personal collection of around 40 boards on my wall. I've tested and used probably over a hundred boards, and probably edited the reviews of a hundred. In short, Tom's Guide senior writer Nikita and I test a lot of keyboards. And we have to give them away when we're done.

One of the main questions I ask people is, "do you want a mechanical keyboard or magnetic keyboard?" And the main response I get is, "what's the difference?"

In simple terms, it comes down to whether you're mostly gaming or typing. But like most things in life, the reality is a little more nuanced than that. Here's what you need to know, with a few of my top suggestions sprinkled in along the way.

The Keychron K2 HE is a magnetic keyboard, with tons of gaming features. But it's gasket mounted, making it extremely comfortable to type on for long periods of time. I should know, as I reviewed it, and I still use it for work on a regular basis as part of my keyboard rotation.

The non-halo version of my beloved NuPhy Halo75 V2, the Node75 ticks many of the same boxes. Beautiful styling, beautiful switches, beautiful keycap profile. I awarded the Node75 a full five stars in my review. It really is that good, especially for the money. And now it's even cheaper.

The main differences come down to whether you need certain gaming features, or whether you want a certain typing feel. However, there are some extra considerations to make... like sound.

The most compelling reason to buy a magnetic keyboard is for the gaming features. Magnetic switches actuate via magnetic resistance rather than a physical mechanism, so aren't tied down to a single fixed actuation point (i.e. a key depression point where the input is triggered). This opens up a plethora of awesome gaming features that you won't find even on a high-end mechanical gaming keyboard.

There's adjustable actuation, so you can set your keys to actuate with as little as 0.1mm of input. Multiple actuations per keystroke are also possible: you can set the W key so that halfway down is walk, and fully down is actually bound to Shift+W, so run.

And many keyboard manufacturers like Keychron and NuPhy have introduced other cool features that take advantage of magnetic detection, like NuPhy's 'Mod Tap', which changes the input based on how hard/fast you press the key.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

"What about Rapid Trigger?" I hear you call. "And Snap Tap?". I'm gettin' there! 'Rapid Trigger' allows repeat actuations without needing to recycle the switch fully to its reset point — you can basically spam faster. That's not physically possible on a mechanical switch, despite some manufacturers claiming their mechanical keyboards do it.

Last Key Prioritization, A.K.A. 'Snap Tap' is possible on a mechanical keyboard. This is a type of SOCD (simultaneous opposing cardinal direction) resolution. In other words: what the keyboard does when two opposites are inputted at the same time. 'Snap Tap' is just one of a few resolutions to this, and tells the board to prioritize the last key pressed, facilitating quick and easy counter strafing in games with interia-based accuracy penalties like "Valorant" and "Counter-Strike 2" (where it'll get you kicked). You can do this via firmware on a mechanical keyboard.

That doesn't mean mechanical switches are bad for gaming. Unless you're actually going to use any of the above features, ultra-snappy mechanical switches are perfectly fine for most casual and even some competitive gaming. They just don't offer you all the fancy bells and whistles of their magnetic counterparts.

Now, I've been rather pro-magnetic so far, haven't I. This is where the tables are turned. When it comes to typing experience, at least for now, traditional mechanical switches really have a leg up over magnetic. And it all comes down to how switches feel under your finger.

Mechanical switches offer a much more tactile experience, giving you feedback under your fingers. And I'm not just talking about 'Tactile' switches that have a mechanical bump. Even linear mechanical switches (with no mechanical bump) can give you a feeling different to magnetic switches, because they're typically designed with feel in mind — different weightings, springs and such will all affect how a linear switch feels.

In short, this makes typing more enjoyable. That said, there are some upsides to magnetic switches for typing. Adjustable actuation is the main benefit. You can dial in actuation points to wherever is best for you, which allows you to be as fast and accurate as possible. For example, I make far fewer mistakes at 2.6mm actuation, which in turn increases my type speeds as much as 5-10 words per minute. So I set all magnetic keyboards to 2.6mm when type testing (and usually have a work profile using 2.6mm).

There's a spanner in the works these days, too. Manufacturers are now launching true hybrid keyboards that can hot swap between both mechanical and magnetic switches. While Keychron and Gateron have recently launched the first (that I know of) tactile magnetic switch, giving the bumpy feel of a traditional mechanical tactile switch but the gaming features of a magnetic one. Up to now, all magnetic switches have been linear and smooth in operation — it's always felt a bit soulless to a tactile mechanical fan.

For now, though, there's still a much wider array of mechanical switches on offer, with different weights, feels and characteristics. So for typists interested in how their keyboard feels, I'd still recommend mechanical.

You'll also want to consider some other criteria. Mechanical keyboards designed with typing rather than gaming in mind tend to be more comfortable. They often use gasket mounts (where the PCB, switches and keycaps are suspended on rubber gaskets) which give you a comfy, bouncy feeling under your fingers.

Some gaming keyboards, or hybrid boards, use gasket mounts. Typically, though, performance magnetic gaming keyboards will use firmer mounts (top, plate, or tray mounts), which move about less. If your actuation is triggered in 0.1mm increments, you don't want your switches wobbling about.

Similarly, looks aren't really part of this debate, as any keyboard can be styled well or otherwise. Typically, though, custom mechanical keyboards tend to be designed with styling as a prime consideration, and therefore look a little more fun (speaking very generally).

Then, of course, there's sound. With the wider array of switches available on the market, and the fact they're built for the custom enthusiast market, mechanical boards tend to sound better. But there are bland examples found in both genres.

Finally, there's poll rates. But this is a bit of a non-issue. 8K polling is found on both magnetic and mechanical keyboards, but it's mostly snake oil. 1,000Hz found on many mechanical boards is more than enough for low latency gaming and to minimize the chance of missed inputs.

My primary advice here is this: just consider what you actually need. Don't be suckered in by all the marketing talk and fancy features. And don't think price is an issue. You can pick up magnetic and mechanical keyboards for under $50.

Are you going to be doing lots of competitive gaming where you need cutting edge performance features? If so, get a magnetic keyboard.

Do you care about a beautiful experience under your fingers? If so, you can consider a mechanical keyboard with lovely switches, or the ability to hot-swap between them. If you don't care about purist type-feel and just want raw speed and accuracy, a magnetic keyboard might still be best for heavy typists.

And here's the curve ball. Do you want the best of both? Then invest in a dual MX/HE keyboard, but be prepared to spend big bucks.

The Keychron K2 HE is a magnetic keyboard, with tons of gaming features. But it's gasket mounted, making it extremely comfortable to type on for long periods of time. I should know, as I reviewed it, and I still use it for work on a regular basis as part of my keyboard rotation.

In terms of sheer performance and polish versus cost, the NuPhy Air60 HE is my top Hall Effect gaming keyboard. It's a lot cheaper than the venerated Wooting 60HE+, yet offers just as many features and the companion software, NuPhy.io is (almost) as slick as Wooting's. For the money, though, this would be my pick. If you don't like low-profile, you could also check out the NuPhy FIeld75 HE.

This keyboard is a bit of a shameless rip off of the Wooting 60HE+... even down to the strap accessory. I haven't tested this exact model, but I have tested its bigger sibling, the HE75 Mag, and for under $50, these magnetic boards rule. You won't get the software polish of the Wooting board the HE60 emulates, or indeed of NuPhy or Keychron, but this is a budget pick after all... you can't have everything at this price.

The non-halo version of my beloved NuPhy Halo75 V2, the Node75 ticks many of the same boxes. Beautiful styling, beautiful switches, beautiful keycap profile. I awarded the Node75 a full five stars in my review. It really is that good, especially for the money. And now it's even cheaper.

The Rainy 75 Pro is probably the best sounding keyboard we've tested. It was so good that, even though my colleague reviewed it, I had to get one for myself. It's an absolute dream to type on too, thanks to the Kailh Cocoa switches.

If you're after a competent all-rounder mechanical board for typing and gaming on a budget, the Keychron C1 Pro 8K is my suggestion. This board is crazy cheap given its performance, switches and styling. The perfect entry-level mechanical board, if you ask me.

Discount with coupon! Remember when I said hybrid MX/HE boards don't come cheap? Yeah, the Lofree Hyzen is about as cheap as they come right now. Your other option is the slightly cheaper Keychron V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE, which is a better board and comes with a tactile magnetic switch, but it's still in pre-order until December.

Amazon has cut prices across its entire Fire TV Soundbar lineup for Black Friday, with discounts covering everything from a basic two-channel soundbar designed to improve on your TV's built-in speakers to a full 5.1-channel setup with a wireless subwoofer and rear surround speakers. For more on the sale, you can also check out our Black Friday deals page, where we're covering the latest discounts ahead of this year's event.

Amazon Fire TV Soundbar is $74.99 (was $119.99), making it the least expensive option in the lineup for anyone who wants a step up from TV speakers for everyday viewing—it's a 24-inch, two-channel bar that supports DTS Virtual:X and Dolby Audio, though it doesn’t have Dolby Atmos or a separate subwoofer. Despite its name, it's an audio-only soundbar and requires a Fire TV streaming stick for you to get any of the Fire TV experience. For more on this soundbar, read PCMag’s review.

Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus is down to $139.99 from $249.99, and the extra money over the base model gets you a dedicated center channel that helps make dialogue easier to follow, along with a built-in subwoofer, Dolby Atmos, and DTS:X support. That said, it doesn’t have up-firing drivers, so the Atmos effect stays largely horizontal, but the center channel does real work on mumbled dialogue in prestige dramas. As with the base model, this one also handles audio only and needs a Fire TV device for any of the streaming features. This PCMag review has more detail on how it performs.

Amazon Fire TV Soundbar with Alexa Voice Remote Pro is $109.98 (was $154.98). This pairs the entry-level bar with the upgraded remote, which adds backlit buttons, two customizable shortcuts you can set for favorite apps or Alexa commands, and a remote finder (for when it inevitably disappears into the couch). If you don’t specifically want or need the remote, though, the Soundbar Plus is a more capable soundbar for just $30 more.

Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer is $229.99, down from $374.99. This configuration takes the same 3.1-channel bar and pairs it with a separate wireless subwoofer, which gives bass-heavy scenes and film scores considerably more weight than the bar's built-in woofer can manage on its own—and at $90 more than the discounted Soundbar Plus, this is the option I'd consider if fuller bass is a priority. Keep in mind that it doesn't add rear speakers, so you're still working with a 3.1 setup and sound that stays in front of you.

Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer and Surround Sound Speakers is $349.99, down from $489.99. This is the complete 5.1 package, adding two rear speakers to the 3.1 bar and wireless subwoofer, so action scenes and other surround effects come from behind you, rather than only from the direction of the TV—but it costs $120 more than the discounted soundbar and subwoofer bundle, so it’s worth considering how much you want that surround-sound effect. Also, while the rear speakers connect to the soundbar wirelessly, each still needs a power outlet.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.
