AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?

AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.

The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.

Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.

Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”

In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”

These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Superintelligence Delusion.”

#3255. Proton Pass is up to 60% off for Black Friday, and it does way more than just store your passwords

There’s a familiar interruption that comes with shopping online: you’ve found what you want, you’re ready to check out, and the store asks you to sign in. Was this the account with your usual password? Did you change it last time? Is it easier to reset it again?

Proton Pass is designed to take that friction out of your day. It creates strong, unique passwords, remembers them for you, and fills them in when you log in. But it also handles something a password alone can’t: keeping your real email address out of another retailer’s database.

For Black Friday, Proton Pass Plus and Pass Family are both 60% off their regular monthly pricing with a one-year subscription, while Proton Unlimited is 50% off. Pass Plus starts at $1.99 per month, billed annually, making this a good opportunity to get your passwords — and a few other important parts of your digital life — organized.

Take a look at Proton’s Black Friday offers, starting at $1.99 per month

The problem with strong passwords isn’t understanding why you need them; it’s keeping track of a different one for every account.

Proton Pass does that work for you. When you sign up for a website, its password generator can create a strong password that’s completely unique. Save it in your vault, and Proton Pass can fill in your credentials when you return.

That’s useful whether you’re creating an account for a single purchase or signing into a service you use every day.

Unique passwords also help limit the fallout from a data breach. If a retailer exposes your login credentials, using a different password elsewhere means those same credentials won’t unlock your other accounts.

With unlimited logins and encrypted vaults that sync across devices, Proton Pass lets you keep those details together as you move between your phone and computer.

Proton Pass is available for practically every platform, from Chrome and Firefox on the web to native macOS, Windows, and Linux apps to, of course, iOS and Android. This makes it trivially easy to access your passwords, passkeys, and API credentials wherever you find yourself.

Black Friday shopping often leaves something behind long after the packages arrive: a steady stream of promotional emails from stores you barely remember visiting.

Proton Pass includes unlimited hide-my-email aliases, giving you an alternative to handing out your real address every time you create an account.

An alias is an extra email address that forwards messages to your normal inbox. You can give it to a shopping website and still receive your order confirmations and delivery updates, without sharing the underlying address you use for everything else.

If that alias starts receiving spam, you can switch it off. Your real email address stays the same, and you don’t have to update all your other accounts.

It’s a practical way to put some distance between your primary inbox and the websites you’re trying for the first time. A separate alias for each service also gives you more control: you can stop messages arriving through one address without disrupting the others.

Passwords are only part of what’s worth keeping in a secure, accessible place.

Proton Pass also stores notes, credit card details, and other confidential information in end-to-end encrypted vaults. That makes it useful for the small, everyday moments when you need something sensitive and don’t want to go looking for it.

When you’re booking a flight, saved passport details let you look up the information you need without digging through a drawer halfway through the reservation.

When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

When you’re traveling, keeping a digital copy of an important document within reach gives you a convenient reference while you’re away from home. It doesn’t replace an original document where one is required, but it can save you from searching through scattered files and messages.

Pass Plus also includes a built-in two-factor authenticator, Dark Web Monitoring, and secure link and vault sharing. Those features give you more ways to manage access to your accounts and share sensitive information when you need to.

Pass Plus is the straightforward choice for one person who wants password generation, autofill, unlimited aliases, and secure storage.

Pass Family includes six Pass Plus accounts and a family admin panel. If several people in your household need a password manager, it’s worth considering rather than setting everyone up with separate subscriptions.

Proton Unlimited bundles Pass with Proton VPN, Proton Mail, Proton Drive, and more, including 500 GB of cloud storage. It’s the option to consider if you also want a VPN, encrypted email, and cloud storage alongside your password manager.

A password manager isn’t the most conspicuous Black Friday purchase, but it’s one you can put to work immediately: the next account you create, the next password you forget, or the next time a checkout asks for details you don’t have handy.

#3254. Netflix Edits Schizophrenia Scene Out Of Tyson Fury Doc After Wife Reveals Boxer Does Not Have Condition

Tyson Fury does not have schizophrenia and a scene in which his wife claims he does has been edited out of the Netflix movie about the British boxing superstar.

The doc, titled Tyson Fury, provides a tell-all account of Fury’s mental health struggles as he builds up to his fight with Anthony Joshua next month, which is also on Netflix.

The trailer initially showed Fury’s wife Paris Fury saying the boxer is a “mild schizophrenic,” but amid questions from the boxing regulator, this has now been revealed to be untrue. Related Stories News Netflix Tunes Into Music-Driven Chinese Fantasy Series 'The Melody Of Love' News Netflix Posts Racy Thanksgiving Message On 'The Hunting Wives' Season 2 Premiere Day

“I want to clarify a statement I made in the original version of the Tyson Fury documentary,” a statement from Paris Fury said. “I recalled a conversation from many years ago when discussing Tyson’s condition and I used the word ‘schizophrenic.’ While Tyson did show some symptoms associated with schizophrenia, he doesn’t have this condition and has never received a diagnosis.” Watch on Deadline

A Netflix spokeswoman said the scene has been removed from the doc, which dropped today.

“Following new information shared by the family relating to Tyson’s official mental health diagnosis, we have worked alongside them to update the documentary accordingly ahead of launch,” she added.

Following the schizophrenia comments, which were also included in a Netflix press release about the doc on Monday, the British Boxing Board of Control said it had been examining whether what was thought to be Fury’s diagnosis would get in the way of his long-anticipated fight with fellow British boxer Joshua.

That fight has now been cleared to take place on December 11 in Cardiff and could prove to be one of Netflix’s most lucrative live sporting events.

Fury’s doc is billed as a “raw, real, unfiltered” look at “the man behind the boxing icon.” Fury has also appeared in two seasons of Netflix’s ob-doc At Home With the Furys, with a third in motion. Both the feature doc and TV show are produced by Banijay-backed Optomen.

#3253. Check out this beautiful wallpaper to celebrate the opening of the latest Apple Store

Apple has quietly announced the upcoming opening of its latest retail store in Hyderabad, India. Located at the Lakeshore Mall in Kukatpally, it opens at 5pm on Thursday, December 10.

As is now usual, the company has created some exclusive wallpaper to mark the event, and you can download it for iPhone, iPad, and Mac …

The store will be the seventh one to open in India. There’s no press release or photos as yet – the company has simply quietly added the store to its list in the country.

As we’ve previously explained, Apple had been trying to open retail stores in India since at least 2015, but had to undertake a lengthy battle with the government before finally being allowed to do so in 2023. Since then, the company has averaged two new stores a year.

India has taken a clever approach to economic development, offering both incentives to establish local manufacturing plants, and barriers to imports of foreign-made products. That carrot-and-stick approach has proven successful, with companies like Apple jumping through the necessary hoops in order to sell their products to the second largest population in the world.

An India First initiative required companies to manufacture a significant proportion of their products within the country in order to avoid high import tariffs. This forced Apple, Samsung, and other companies to establish manufacturing plants in India, bringing jobs to the country.

Additionally, India does not allow company-branded retail stores unless the same conditions are met. That particular requirement was mostly intended to target Apple.

The plan worked, with Apple asking its suppliers and iPhone assemblers to establish manufacturing plants within India. Initially, that was just for the iPhone SE, but more advanced phones have gradually been added, and today the country is the second largest manufacturing base after China. All iPhones sold in the US are made in India.

Apple has for some time now created unique wallpapers to mark the opening of each new store, and the latest example is particularly beautiful.

To download it, you need to visit this page on the device for which you want to use it. For example, if you visit the page on a Mac, you will automatically be taken to the desktop version.

#3251. Community-Focused Academic Brings AI Tools to Colorado Farmers

This senior member’s chatbot helps them start agritourism businesses

Willie Jones covers transportation for IEEE Spectrum and the history of technology for The Institute.

Alice Dong has created an AI chatbot website that helps Colorado farmers plan and operate agribusinesses that draw visitors to their properties.

Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job.

Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension, CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there.

Xue “Alice” Dong Employer Colorado State University Extension in Logan CountyTitle Extension regional specialistMember grade Senior memberAlma maters Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

Colorado State University Extension in Logan County

Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products.

Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business.

She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside.

“We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in.

Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and theU.N.’s International Telecommunication Union, and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC), and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP).

She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture.

Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors.

As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs.

That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings.

“I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says.

She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career.

She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education.

She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016.

That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020.

After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College, in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator.

She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water.

She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain, helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park.

In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns.

She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds.

Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System, a nationwide network run by land-grant universities, schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states.

The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture, managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties.

The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program, which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship.

Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person.

She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says.

“We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says.

Dong also focuses not on only on whether people use AI, but also on how they use it. In 2026, she and Paul Hill from Utah State University Extension published “From Access to Governance: Generative AI Literacy for Extension Professionals and Small Businesses, and a Governance-Aware Design Framework” in the journal AI. The paper offers a framework for helping Extension professionals and small businesses adopt generative AI responsibly.

In 2025, Dong earned a third master’s degree, in artificial intelligence and machine learning, from CSU Global.

She immediately put those skills to work on agritourism, she says. She built the chatbot in Python, a popular programming language. It answers typed questions, and its user interface looks much like ChatGPT’s, but it works differently. Under the hood, it uses retrieval-augmented generation, a technique that has the AI look up information in a set of trusted documents before it answers. Dong curated that collection from Extension publications, so the chatbot’s answers rest on authoritative sources and are less likely to be made up. She presented the project at NeurIPS 2025 (Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems). The code is openly available on GitHub, so other Extension offices can adapt it.

The bot runs in a web browser rather than as a phone app. Many farmers she works with don’t own a smartphone, Dong says, but nearly all have a computer, tablet, or other gadget that can connect to a website. The bot works on any of them, with no app to download.

Extension specialists “act as a bridge. We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Farmers often ask the bot how to attract visitors and how to write a business plan. A farmer thinking about opening a corn maze, for example, can ask how to price admission, what kind of insurance to carry, and which permits to get. The bot also gives advice on managing risk.

One of her test sites was Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch, in eastern Colorado. Dong documented how the ranch put AI to work in a peer-reviewed case study, “Revolutionizing Agritourism with AI and Machine Learning: A Case Study of Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch in Colorado,” published in 2025 in CABI Tourism Cases.

Surveys and interviews she conducted with other users showed that people find it’s easy to use the bot, learn from it, and act on its advice, she says. She is preparing the full results for publication.

Her work extends beyond agritourism. In 2026, she contributed an AI assistant to Project Pythia, an open-science program funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and led by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR). The AI assistant turns raw airport weather report data into plain-language guidance for farmers and other non-technical users, and it tells users when data is missing rather than guessing.

She also teaches workshops on AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. She has taught her workshop 20 times to more than 200 entrepreneurs and business owners, who came from 32 Colorado counties. In follow-up surveys, 90 percent of participants reported trying at least one new AI task in their business. Some of the workshops take place at a community center run by the Logan County Economic Development Corp., in Sterling. She has also co-hosted the workshops with the Rural Community Assistance Corp., Colorado Startup Week, and Boulder Startup Week. And she occasionally presents them as webinars, so people don’t have to travel.

Her outreach has taught her that many farmers are eager to try new tools, she says. She shows them how simple her chatbot is to use.

She also offers advice to high school students drawn to the field. Extension specialists each have a specialty, such as livestock, natural resources, food systems, or 4-H. Students should pick one based on their passion, she says.

Land-grant universities offer related programs at the bachelor’s and master’s levels. For graduate students, she adds, Extension offers a third career path beyond academia and industry: “You apply advanced skills directly to the communities that need them.”

Dong joined IEEE in 2025 and soon was elevated to senior member. Her professional home is the IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology. She also serves as vice treasurer of the IEEE Denver Section’s Young Professionals group.

IEEE supports all three parts of her job, she says. For research, she presented “Entrepreneur AI Agent: Empowering Small Businesses and Bridging the Digital Divide through Context-Aware Generative AI” at the 2026 IEEE Global Humanitarian Technology Conference (GHTC). For teaching, she has offered to bring her AI workshop to Denver Section members and local entrepreneurs. For service, she reviews papers for IEEE conferences.

IEEE conferences matter most to her, she says: “Through them, I can present my research and network with other researchers in the field.”

She attended the IEEE World Forum on Public Safety Technology in Boulder, Colo., in September 2026. The event, she says, opened her eyes to many new projects underway across IEEE.

Still, she says, her work always points back to the farms and ranches of eastern Colorado. Its people are curious, she says, but they can’t make the leap to new technology alone.

“They really need this kind of a bridge,” she says.

Willie Jones is an associate editor at IEEE Spectrum. In addition to editing and planning daily coverage, he manages several of Spectrum's newsletters and contributes regularly to the monthly Big Picture section that appears in the print edition.

For that price, you're doubling the storage of a standard Paperwhite and getting wireless charging, an ad-free lock screen, and a front light that automatically adjusts to your surroundings—on top of the same sharp seven-inch display, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life as the standard Paperwhite, as noted by this PCMag review.

The Like-New Kindle Scribe (16GB) is down to $251.99 from $359.99, the biggest dollar discount in this roundup. Unlike the other Kindles here, it's built for reading and writing, with a 10.2-inch, 300ppi glare-free display and a Premium Pen with an eraser and shortcut button—making it the most versatile option for readers who want an e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3248. Federal Incentive Will Level The Playing Field For America’s Creatives — Guest Column

Editor’s note: Ruth Vitale, who previously held top posts at Paramount Classics, Fine Line Features and New Line Cinema, is CEO of CreativeFuture, a nonprofit coalition of more than 500 companies and organizations and nearly 300,000 individuals devoted to promoting the value of creativity in the digital age.

For more than a decade, CreativeFuture has fought for one simple idea: Members of our creative communities deserve to make a living from the work they create. We have taken on piracy. We have taken on Big Tech. We have taken on criminal enterprises that profit from the theft of our movies, television, music, and books. Related Stories News Trump's "Noisy Name-Calling" Mocked By NYT After Bored POTUS Starts Thanksgiving Ranting Against Reporter's Nvidia Dispatch News Jane Fonda, Robert De Niro & Other Figures Sign Letter Backing Chris Van Hollen For Majority Leader --- Amid A Chuck Schumer Aide's Prank

But right now, America’s creative community faces a different kind of threat. Fewer movies and television shows are being produced in this country. Copyright protects creative work once it exists. It does nothing for the American crews who never got the opportunity to make it. Watch on Deadline

I have spent my entire career in this business – at Vestron, where we made Dirty Dancing, and then at United Artists, Fine Line Features, and Paramount Classics, where we released films like Child’s Play, Road House, Shine, You Can Count on Me, and Hustle & Flow. I have watched independent filmmakers scrape together budgets one dollar at a time. Today, I hear the same question from filmmakers repeatedly: Can we afford to make this in America?

At least 65 countries now offer national production incentives, sometimes in addition to local or regional ones. The United States does not. Thirty-nine states have built programs of their own, but a state program cannot outbid a government overseas with more competitive incentives in place, and the numbers show it. America’s share of global film production has fallen from 52% in 2022, to just 38% at the start of 2026. The share was 65% just over a decade ago.

Let’s be clear about who pays the price. Film and television support more than two million American jobs and pay over $200 billion in wages a year. Nationally, the industry supports 162,000 businesses, 93% of which employ fewer than 10 people.

Those paychecks go to editors and composers, costume designers and carpenters, camera operators and writers’ assistants. Many of them work from project to project, with no guarantee there will be a next one. When a production moves overseas, their jobs move without them.

That is why I am so encouraged by the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act (MPTERA). Introduced last month with strong bipartisan support in both chambers, it would create federal tax relief for film and television made in America based on the U.S. jobs created, including for postproduction and visual effects. Editing suites and effects houses can be anywhere in the world – which means they can just as easily be somewhere other than here.

MPTERA also gives independent productions extra relief, up to 30% of the amount spent on U.S. jobs. As someone who has built much of my career championing independent film, I can tell you that matters. Independent films are where new voices are discovered, and run on margins so thin that an overseas incentive can decide whether they get shot in Albuquerque or Belfast. Or whether they get shot at all.

The upside is enormous. A new study estimates that a federal incentive would support an average of more than 143,000 jobs a year and generate nearly $250 billion in additional economic activity over eight years. And this won’t help only California and New York – our industry is in every state of the union, leaving its economic mark everywhere it goes. There is also a bonus for productions in rural areas or for producers that film in at least 10 states in a year. And keep in mind, a feature film’s location shoot generates an average of $670,000 per day for local communities. For a one-hour television episode, it’s $475,000 per day.

Bottom line: This is not a giveaway. Not a single taxpayer dollar goes to the production – the legislation simply reduces the tax liability of U.S. productions. It is a smart investment in one of the few industries where America still leads the world. Our film and television industry maintains a trade surplus with nearly every nation on Earth. When Americans were asked what their country does better than any other, 58% named movies and television as their top answer. Why would we let that slip away?

Other countries have quickly realized the economic benefit that production brings. Standing still here at home is not a policy. It is clearly a forfeit. This is a bill that has the support of President Trump, as well as Senators Tim Scott and Adam Schiff and Reps. Nathaniel Moran and Linda Sánchez, and 90 other members of Congress. This is the rare bill that has reached across the aisle and to the White House. That doesn’t happen often.

Congress should pass MPTERA this year. We already have the talent and resources and will see the benefit immediately. America’s creatives are ready to work. Let’s give them the chance to do it here at home.

Ruth Vitale is the CEO of CreativeFuture, a nonprofit coalition of over 500 companies and organizations and nearly 300,000 individuals devoted to promoting the value of creativity in the digital age. She has held top posts at Paramount Classics, Fine Line Features, and New Line Cinema.

#3247. I Don’t Trust Visual Recordings Anymore. But One Day I Will Again

We will have to label our content to prove its authenticity

Hany Farid is a computer science professor at Dartmouth College, in Hanover, N.H.

In March of this year, a flurry of emails and text messages from a half dozen reporters around the world disrupted my quiet Saturday morning. An Iranian news agency had aired a week-old video of what appeared to be a U.S.-made Tomahawk missile hitting a school. News reports claimed that the strike killed more than 175 people, most of them children. The U.S. president and military denied responsibility. In the age of generative AI and all things deepfake, everyone—including me—was skeptical of the video’s authenticity.

I get this type of request a lot. For the past three decades, I’ve been developing mathematical and computational techniques to analyze and detect manipulation in digital media. Over this time, I think it’s fair to say that I, like most people, have approached visual recordings with a “presumption of authenticity”: If a skeptic claims that a recording is fake, the burden of proof is on them.

In today’s world of generative AI, however, I think we need to shift this stance to a “presumption of fake.” That is, the burden is now on the creator to prove that their content is real. While this new stance may seem unfair to legitimate creators, I think it both reflects reality and points to a future where we will once again be able to trust that most online media is what it appears to be.

Even last March, I was already tilting toward a presumption of fake. My initial response to the reporters was something along the lines of, “I am suspicious of the video because the quality is low, it emerged weeks after the bombing, and it is only being distributed by an Iranian news agency with a less-than-stellar record of accurate reporting.”

Given the potential implications—if the video was indeed real, however, I resigned myself to spending my Saturday morning analyzing it.

I first reasoned that if the Tomahawk missile was digitally added to each frame of the video without taking into consideration the camera motion, we might see a physically implausible missile path. So I aligned the video frames using a stationary background landmark as a reference. In the updated video, the missile did, in fact, move in a nearly linear trajectory. (See the yellow dots in the composite shown below.)

I next asked if the size (in pixels) of the missile in the video was plausible. Under some reasonable assumptions, I estimated that the missile in the video corresponded to a 6-meter Tomahawk at a distance of approximately 100 meters. The distance seemed plausible from the scene and was also consistent with the delay of 0.3 seconds from visible impact to the sound of impact, given that sound travels at 343 meters per second.

A composite photo composed of frames from a video of the Tomahawk strike reveals the missile’s trajectory.Hany Farid; Source: Mehr News

Despite the mounting evidence, though, I struggled to refine my answer for the reporters.

My skepticism was fueled by a recent study I worked on with colleagues at the University of California, Berkeley, that showed how hard it is to distinguish real from fake videos. Observers are now so suspicious of videos in general that they have trouble convincing themselves that a video is real.

But after a few more hours and a few more analyses with the missile video, I finally decided that it was authentic, and I gave the reporters my updated view.

This analysis marked a turning point for me. I realized I was just like the participants in our study: The lack of artifacts was not enough to readily convince me a video is real. I had flipped from a presumption of real to a presumption of fake.

When the visual record is no longer reliable, what can we do?

The types of forensic analyses that I routinely perform do not currently operate at internet scale and speed. But provenance signals can. These signals include content credentials and watermarks that are inserted or embedded at the time of creation or recording.

Credentials that follow the C2PA standard, for example, attach a cryptographically signed manifest to a photo or video at the moment of capture; this metadata records the device, the time and location of the recording, and any subsequent edits. Because the manifest is signed, any tampering with either the content or its history can be detected later by machine. Watermarks, like Google’s SynthID, embed an imperceptible signal directly into the pixels or audio samples that identifies the content’s origin.

Apple recently took these ideas a step further. On some of its newest iPhones, the camera sensor can cryptographically sign the raw pixel data as it’s captured. That signed data is then developed into a reference image saved alongside the normal, editable photo. Anyone can then compare the two and see exactly what, if anything, was changed.

These provenance signals are often criticized as being only a partial solution or vulnerable to attack. This is true if we think of them as mechanisms for catching bad actors. But that’s not what they’re supposed to do. Their purpose is to let good actors prove that their audiovisual recording is what it claims to be.

Provenance signals thus need not be adversary-proof. Instead, these signals are part of a new reality in which consumers, journalists, and the courts must adapt to a presumption of fakeness. If enough good actors adopt these mechanisms, they can begin to drown out bad actors. In other words, we have to switch from a model of “catch the bad actors” to “empower the good actors.”

This switch from trust to distrust of digital media has expanded to include routine video calls.

In September 2024, for example, Senator Ben Cardin (D-Md.), then chair of the Foreign Relations Committee, received a video meeting request from Dmytro Kuleba, who until a few weeks earlier had been Ukraine’s foreign minister. During the call, Cardin became suspicious when, out of character, Kuleba pressed him on whether the U.S. should allow Ukraine to fire long-range missiles into Russia. Cardin ended the call. Later, the State Department confirmed that Kuleba had never requested the meeting, and the Senate security office warned staff that foreign adversaries, possibly Russian, would likely try similar faked meetings again.

All it takes to conduct this type of impersonation is a face swap or avatar deepfake, along with voice conversion, both of which substitute the speaker’s face and voice for deepfaked versions in real time. These technologies are readily available in commercial products and open-source libraries and run on nothing more powerful than a modern laptop.

This video illustrates the current state of face-swap deepfakes.

Farid’s Company GetReal Shows How Real Deepfake Videos Look Today Your browser does not support the video tag. Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetReal

Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetReal

Unlike the Tomahawk video, which I could sit with for a morning analyzing frame by frame, a live video call offers no time for human analysis. On the other hand, real-time deepfakes pose new challenges for their creators: A fake video call has to be generated at around 24 frames per second to fool the eye into perceiving realistic motion. As a result, the deepfake-video-call software has to take shortcuts, such as simplifying faces and how they interact with their surroundings, and allowing some drift between audio and video or between video frames. The human eye doesn’t notice the shortcuts, but we can forensically expose them.

Provenance signals should eventually play a role here. Video-calling software could apply the same cryptographic signing to each frame of a live video stream that Apple now applies to still photographs. A face swap necessarily occurs between a speaker’s camera and the videoconferencing software, and so the software could verify in real time whether the frames it’s receiving were signed by a physical camera sensor or whether they were altered in transit. As before, the burden shifts from catching the impersonator to allowing real participants to prove they are who they claim to be.

For the first two decades of the digital revolution, forensic analysis—finding the telltale traces of manipulation—was enough to adjudicate most questions of authenticity. The AI revolution, however, has changed the scale and speed of manipulation beyond what forensics alone can handle. To believe a recording is real now, it must also carry a provenance signal from the point of recording. The two approaches work together, with provenance allowing good actors to be trusted, while forensic analyses root out the bad actors.

Hany Farid is a computer science professor at Dartmouth College, in Hanover, N.H. About 10 years ago, he randomly picked up a book in the library on the federal rules of evidence and was astonished to learn that courts made no distinction between photos from negatives and digital photos, even though the latter can be easily altered. “Digital photography was just getting started,” Farid says. “I realized this was really going to be a huge problem.” Since then digital photo forensics has become the focus of his research. He now frequently testifies in U.S. courts and advises law enforcement agencies. “All that from picking up a book,” he says.

The emerging authentication and provenance systems make a lot of sense for mainstream uses. I get the impression we'll still need forensic analysis for plenty of edge cases, though. People using older hardware or anyone trying to capture evidence in situations where it isn't safe to share clues about the media's origin come to mind.

Still a bit more robust result here on a limited basis than Wake Up Dead Man ($4.25M 5-day), but alas, Netflix, you’re leaving soooo much money on the table and there’s more than a enough room in this marketplace to have gone wide and minted at least $20M for this sequel to beloved fan Quentin Tarantino pic Once Upon a Time in Hollywood which at $142.8M is the Oscar winning filmmaker’s second highest grossing movie at the domestic B.O. Cliff Booth filmmaker David Fincher told Collider that the pic cost $120M-$123M, not $200M. We’ll leave it to Wall Street to figure out the downstream.

There’s a shot that Neon’s third weekend wide expansion of James Gray’s crime noir, Paper Tiger, based on the filmmaker’s life, comes in higher than Cliff Booth. Wednesday was an estimated $950K which translates into a $4.4M 3-day, 5-day of $5.1M at 1,322 (+1,294) theaters. Running total by Sunday is around $5.7M. Audiences weren’t wild about the Miles Teller, Adam Driver and Scarlett Johansson movie giving it a C+.

Angel Studio’s Hershey biopic about the chocolate maker with Alexandra Daddario and Finn Wittrock got a leg up with early shows yesterday with $1.3M including $534K estimated previews. No firm projection yet, but it was always expected to file in the single digits over its ‘4-day’ start. The pic doesn’t officially open until Thursday and all that preview cash will be rolled into day one. CinemaScore audiences love it with an A, and PostTrak isn’t shabby with 83% positive and a 69% definite recommend, but critics didn’t have a sweet tooth for it 17% Rotten. Male-to-female turnout was 50/50 with the Angel faithful attending at 37% over 55, and 51% over 45. Diversity demos are 61% Caucasian, 17% Black, 13% Latino and Hispanic, 6% Asian American, and 3% Native American/other.

WEDNESDAY AFTERNOON: If extreme weather doesn’t shutter theaters in the Northeast, then Lionsgate is looking forward to a lucrative Thanksgiving stretch with The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping potentially banking $85M+ over five-days.

Should the sixth title in the Suzanne Collins series file in that range, it will rep the second best Thanksgiving haul for a Hunger Games movie after Catching Fire‘s $109.9M Wednesday-Sunday turkey take 13 years ago. Sunrise on the Reaping‘s Wednesday is looking like $15.5M-$16.5M with a second 3-day weekend around $58M-$65M at 4,018 theaters, -46% to -51%. Five day forecasts are always a challenge for the industry to predict: Business dips on Thanksgiving then spikes on Black Friday, which is one of the most active moviegoing days of the year. By Sunday, we’re looking at a running cume for the Francis Lawrence directed movie of $233M domestic, which would be 40% higher than the lifetime cume on 2023’s Hunger Games: Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes.

Second will either be Disney’s Hexed at 3,725 theaters or Universal/Paramount’s Focker-in-Law at 3,382 sites. Hexed is seeing around $7.8M today (including $2.1M previews), for a 3-day around $20M and 5-day between $35M-$40M. Let’s see if this picks up before passing complete judgement on this $200M original animation production, but it’s clear Hexed isn’t Coco or Frozen.

Focker In-Law is seeing a $5.2M Wednesday, 3-day of $24.8M and 5-day of $36.1M. No Rotten Tomatoes audience scores yet on either title.

Fourth goes to Paramount’s third frame of Johnny Depp Christmas movie, Ebenezer with $1.5M today at 3,180 sites and a 3-day between $6.8M-$7.3M, -6% to -13%, for a 5-day of $10M-$10.6M and running cume on the high end of $45.9M.

Fifth is Amazon MGM Studio’s fourth frame of I Play Rocky at 2,711 with $1.4M today, 3-day of $6.6M, and 5-day of $9.5M for a running cume of $22.5M.

Outside the top 5 is Netflix’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth at 251 locations with $1M today, $3M 3-day and 5-day of $5M.

WEDNESDAY AM: As we told you last night, Lionsgate scored its best Tuesday ever at the domestic box office with The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping and the best ever for the Suzanne Collins franchise as the day raked in $15.98M.

2013’s The Hunger Games: Catching Fire owned the previous best Tuesday for the franchise with $15.96M. Running cume for the fifth Francis Lawrence movie is $148.1M and by Thanksgiving, Sunrise on the Reaping will surpass its previous 2023 chapter’s lifetime domestic B.O. of $166.3M.

As we told you, Sunrise on the Reaping will dominate the Thanksgiving Wednesday through Sunday stretch as the franchise has historically done before since 2013, this time with a floor of $70M+. Previously, the pics over Thanksgiving cooked up the following: Catching Fire ($109.9M), Mockingjay Part 1 ($82.6M), Mockingjay Part 2 ($75.9M) with Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes way behind ($42.2M).

Lionsgate has had back-to-back global hit openings this year with Sunrise on the Reaping last weekend at $226.1M WW and Michael with $218.8M. This has all happened under the administration and watch of Motion Picture Chairman, Adam Fogelson. Still no word out there whether or not Lionsgate rejected or accepted Legendary’s bid.

Walt Disney Animation’s Hexed came in with $2.1M, $100K above the $2M we were spotting yesterday. That preview figure is higher than Encanto ($1.5M previews, 5-day of $40.5M) and Wish ($1.8M previews including $500K Saturday sneaks; 5-day of $31.6M). No RT audience score yet, but critics were meh at 67% fresh. There is a chance that the traditional Disney pic comes in lower than its 5-day forecast of $40M-$45M as original animated titles are very challenging to launch in the streaming era, but you have to start some place.

Universal and Paramount’s Focker In-Law, which didn’t have previews last night, rather began showtimes at midnight, has more potential to hit its 5-day forecast of $45M given the Ariana Grande factor and the fact that audiences love the franchise. The first Meet the Parents 26 years ago was the fave among critics at 85% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Focker-in-Law isn’t the worst at 26%, as that belongs to 2010’s Little Fockers. 2004’s Meet the Fockers stands at 39%.

Hexed, Focker-in-Law and Sunrise on the Reaping are sharing PLFs with the latter having Imax screens (except for AMC where they are being designated to Netflix’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth).

Thank God for Lionsgate Hunger Games at the box office: Sans a Wicked, Moana and a Zootopia, the Thanksgiving box office will certainly be down from last year’s five day robust $290.3M, which was the fifth best ever. Moana 2 and Wicked led the holiday to its best haul ever with $424.9M.

Terrestrial networks cannot reach every location. Oceans, remote regions, and disaster zones often remain without coverage. 5G non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by using satellites and high-altitude platforms. Introduced in 3GPP Release 17, NR-NTN keeps evolving through Releases 18, 19, and 20. Satellite links bring new challenges. Signals travel long distances, satellites move at high speed, and Doppler shift affects synchronization and timing. These effects shape payload design, mobility procedures, and device behavior. They also call for new testing methods for devices, satellites, and networks. This paper explains the technology step by step. It also shows how NTN is shaping unified terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks in 6G.

#3240. These Signature Sony Headphones Are Under $200 During Black Friday

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality currently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

The WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99) during Amazon's early Black Friday sale. That 50% off brings it down to the lowest price they've ever reached, a good deal for premium headphones that still sound incredible, even in 2026.

I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The WH-1000XM5 received an "outstanding" review from PCMag for their top-notch audio quality and exceptional audio when using the best-in-class active noise cancellation. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.

These headphones also have a stereo 3.5mm connection, which is perfect for those who want to use a cable and not worry about battery life. And speaking of battery life, Sony says you can expect about 30 hours, but it will vary depending on your use of ANC. They are compatible with AAC, LDAC, and SBC codecs and have multipoint connection, meaning you can pair them with more than one device at the same time.

Personally, I think the value for the money you get with the XM5 for $198 is better than paying full price for the XM6. If you're looking to get ahead of the Black Friday chaos and secure an amazing deal on great headphones, this is it.

Shot almost entirely on security cameras and iPhones in Hollywood, the short “follows Thom (newcomer Tanner Agpoon-Steinbock), an aspiring musician gigging as a rideshare driver who is asked by a grieving passenger (actress and comedian Alyssa Limperis) to spread her grandmother’s ashes.” Rebecca Metz (Better Things) also stars.

#3236. MacBook Neo vs MacBook Air: Which should you buy right now?

Apple’s Mac lineup is stronger than ever this year, largely thanks to the new MacBook Neo. If you’re deciding between the MacBook Neo and the MacBook Air this holiday season, here’s everything you need to know.

The MacBook Neo is Apple’s most affordable laptop ever, starting at $699 (currently on sale for $599). It features a solid aluminum design that comes in a range of fun colors, including Silver, Blush, Citrus, and Indigo

Unlike Apple’s other Macs, the MacBook Neo is powered by an A-series chip rather than an M-series chip. It uses the A18 Pro chip originally introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro, featuring a 6-core CPU and 5-core GPU.

The MacBook Neo comes with 8GB of unified memory, with no additional RAM configuration options available. It starts with 256GB of storage, with a 512GB configuration available for an additional $100. That $100 upgrade also gets you Touch ID, which is not included in the base model.

There are some other trade-offs compared to the MacBook Air. The MacBook Neo lacks a backlit keyboard, MagSafe charging, and a Force Touch trackpad. It also has more limited USB-C connectivity and supports just one external display.

Still, the MacBook Neo offers an impressive feature set. It has a 13-inch display, up to 16 hours of battery life, a 1080p FaceTime camera, and the full macOS experience.

The MacBook Air, meanwhile, was updated earlier this year with Apple’s M5 chip. It starts at $1,299, making it $600 more expensive than the entry-level MacBook Air. The MacBook Air is currently on sale with a starting price of $999.

For that $600 upgrade, the MacBook Air offers several key advantages over the MacBook Air. The M5 chip has a 10-core CPU and up to a 10-core GPU, enabling better sustained performance than the MacBook Neo.

The MacBook Air also starts with 16GB of unified memory and 512GB of storage, both double the entry-level MacBook Neo. You can configure it with up to 32GB of memory and 4TB of storage, while the MacBook Neo is limited to 8GB of memory and 512GB of storage.

Apple rates the MacBook Air for up to 18 hours of video streaming and 15 hours of wireless web browsing, compared to 16 hours and 11 hours, respectively, for the MacBook Neo.

As I wrote in my review earlier this year, I think the MacBook Neo is a great Mac, full stop … not just because of the great price. It can handle the vast majority of things most people will throw at it. This includes web browsing, basic photo and video editing, research, and much more.

The M5 MacBook Air, meanwhile, offers more power and more configuration options. This makes it a great option for people who need more storage, RAM, and power than the MacBook Neo can offer.

One of my favorite things about the MacBook Air is that it’s available in two screen sizes. The 15-inch MacBook Air is one of my favorite Apple laptops with a combination of the ultra-thin and light design and the larger screen. I think a lot of people forget it exists, but it’s an excellent choice.

To recap, I think the MacBook Neo is a great choice for everyday tasks like web browsing, email, writing, and streaming. The MacBook Air is a better fit for more demanding workflows, including photo and video editing, coding, working with large spreadsheets, and heavy multitasking.

Beyond performance, the MacBook Air offers a handful of niceties that you won’t find on the MacBook Neo. These include a backlit keyboard, a larger display with True Tone, MagSafe charging, a better webcam and speakers, and a Force Touch trackpad. It also includes Touch ID on every configuration, longer battery life, and support for two external displays.

If it’s in the budget, I think the MacBook Air is an excellent choice for all Mac shoppers. It’s plenty powerful, thin and light, and is highly configurable compared to the MacBook Neo.

What do you think of the MacBook Neo vs MacBook Air decision? Which would you choose? Let us know down in the comments.

#3233. Denis Villeneuve “Deeply Disappointed” That ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Will Launch On Same Weekend As ‘Dune: Part Three’

Denis Villeneuve says he is “deeply disappointed” that Disney chose to release box office juggernaut Avengers: Doomsday over the same December 18 weekend as the third instalment in his Dune franchise.

In a new interview with Time Magazine, Villeneuve said his first two Dune films had to contend with the tail end of the pandemic and then the Hollywood strikes, respectively, something he described as “rough” and “not easy”. With the third film, he thought he and Warner Bros were out of the woods. Then came news that Disney was dropping into the same release weekend with Avengers. Related Stories News 'Avengers: Doomsday' U.S. Presales Now At $100M+ As Pic Heads For $270M+ Opening - Box Office News Chris Evans On Secret Meetings About 'Avengers' Return Despite Saying He Was "Happily Retired" From MCU

He expanded: “Disney put the biggest franchise of all time against us. I’m no fool. Those movies are a mammoth. So I was deeply disappointed. But we had committed to this date, to IMAX. It was impossible to move. So I accepted my fate, praying to the gods of cinema. Dune is not a mammoth like the Avengers, but it’s a sexy little animal that has a lot of firepower, and I hope we will survive. It could be one of the biggest box-office weekends of all time because of both movies. Am I in competition with the Avengers? Absolutely not. It’s a T. rex. But I stand proud because I think the film delivers.”” Watch on Deadline

My colleague Anthony had a report earlier this week looking at both films’ domestic box office outlook. NRG tracking has Avengers gunning for a $270M+ start with a shot at $300M and Dune eyeing a $75M-80M start. The former is NRG’s biggest ever opening weekend projection. The latter would be close to Dune: Part Two‘s first domestic weekend.

The Time interview also touched on Villeneuve’s upcoming James Bond film. Villeneuve described his excitement for it: “I don’t sleep a lot right now because it’s like I have electricity in my veins thinking about this new project. It is so different.“

The filmmaker was asked whether he would stick to tradition or look to deviate with his Bond: “I love traditions. I love the unapologetic way the character behaves, the panache. I’m not here to change the DNA of James Bond. I’m here to embrace it, to bring it to the world of today. I’m a hardcore James Bond fan, and I want other fans to have fun watching my film. Of course, it will be tainted by my sensibility. But I wake up every morning with a stupid smile because it’s a world of pure cinematic pleasure.”

The director and interviewer were speaking ahead of the news that Robert Pattinson will be Bond, but Villeneuve acknowledged that whoever they chose wouldn’t please everyone:

“No matter what we do, we will never please everybody. When Daniel Craig was cast, it was a sh-tstorm. He was blond. He was short. He was not seen as an action hero. Yet when we talk about James Bond today it is because of Daniel Craig’s extraordinary interpretation. And that was a different environment in 2006 before social media. I expect a hurricane when we bring our choice to the world. Some people will be happy. Some will be mad. I can do nothing about that. At the end of the day, the truth will be on the screen. Then they will be able to judge.“

#3232. TVs, Laptops, and More of the Best Tech Deals From Sam's Club's Black Friday Sale

Retailers and brands are churning out Black Friday deals, including the likes of Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, Samsung, and others. If you're a Sam's Club member, you have access to many Black Friday deals worth checking out, so I spent some time combing through their website and rounded up my favorite tech deals.

The Bose SoundLink Flex SE is a portable Bluetooth speaker with an IP67 waterproof rating. The speaker even floats in the water, so you can bring it with you into the pool. While it doesn't offer full EQ customization in its companion app, the sound has rich bass depth and clear highs out of the box. It also features a speakerphone, allowing you to take calls and speak with it. It's light and portable, and the Bluetooth 5.3 supports multipoint connectivity and SBC, AAC, and aptX codecs. You can get the Bose 2nd Generation SoundLink Flex SE for $89 (originally $139).

Skullcandy makes fun speakers and headphones, although they're not designed for audiophiles (their sound signature is very bass-heavy). Their Skullcandy Stomp XL Max is their attempt at making a portable party speaker. It comes with two wireless mics, making it a great option for karaoke. It holds 12 hours of battery life (up to 20 hours with certain settings), has an IPX5 water resistance rating, and has LED lights that sync to the music. You can get it for $99 (originally $199).

Getting a soundbar can exponentially improve anyone's entertainment system, but a 5.1 system with rear speakers and a subwoofer takes it to the next level. The Samsung HW-Q65F 5.1 Channel Soundbar is $299 (originally $399), and it's a wireless setup that will keep the harmony of "too many cables" in the house. It supports Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X to give you a 3D audio feel, and it has a dialogue feature that will let you hear the whispers.

These kinds of sales are always a good time to upgrade laptops. If you're looking for a powerful computer that is well-rounded, consider the 16-inch HP OmniBook 7 Flip going for $699 (originally $899). This laptop comes with an Intel Ultra 5 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 16GB of RAM (which, honestly, is the minimum anyone should be buying in 2026).

If you need a bigger screen, the 17.3-inch HP OmniBook 3 is a good choice for a bit less money at $649 (originally $999). It comes with an Intel Core Ultra 7 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 12GB of RAM. Part of the bigger screen means a bigger keyboard, so if you deal with numbers a lot, you'd likely appreciate the numeric pad.

If you want your laptop strictly for gaming, the ASUS TUF F16 Gaming laptop is $1,149 (originally $1,399). With an Intel Core 7 processor and the RTX 5060 graphics card, you'll be well set up to tackle heavy games. It comes with a 165Hz refresh rate, Advanced Arc Flow fans and vents to keep your machine cool, and 16GB DDR5 RAM to keep your loads short.

Gaming monitors can get expensive quickly, but you can get decent options on a budget. A great example is the 31.5-inch MSi gaming monitor selling for $129 (originally $179). It has a 250Hz refresh rate and a 1ms response time to make gaming smoother. There's also AMD FreeSync Premium to get rid of tearing and stuttering.

Budget TVs get big discounts during Black Friday, and the 58-inch Vizio QLED TV is one of them. You can get one for $178 (originally $298), and it supports Dolby Vision HDR for better color and contrast. The operating system is the Vizio OS, but of course, you can always change it with a TV dongle if you prefer a different one.

If you prefer to splurge for a better QLED but still get a good deal, the 65-inch Samsung QN90H QLED TV at $1,197.99 (originally $1,497.99) is a great option. It works for gaming with its 144Hz refresh rate, and because the operating system is Tizen OS, it comes with Samsung TV Plus, which brings over 2,700 free channels. The TV also comes with Dolby Atmos, so you can hear audio with a 3D effect as the audio follows objects around the display.

A 100-inch TV makes a statement: You take your entertainment system seriously. The 100-inch Vizio QLED TV is a budget-friendly option with a $300 discount, currently going for $1,198 (originally $1,498). This TV supports Dolby Vision HDR for more vivid images and has hundreds of free channels with the Vizio OS.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Sam Club's 2026 Black Friday sale runs from November 26 to November 29, 2026, starting online at 12:01 a.m. on Thanksgiving Day, but the deals start even earlier.

Yes, you'll need to be a member to get the deals, but you can shop online without a membership with a 10% surcharge. However, you can always get a year membership for $120, which includes a Walmart+ membership, free shipping, and other perks.

#3231. iOS 28 to ‘revamp’ iPhone notifications, per report

iOS 28 is coming next year, and a new rumor says the update will “revamp the iPhone’s notification system.” This comes as Android has introduced features like “Notification Organizer” to help users sort notifications into different categories.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

The report cites “multiple sources” and comes from MacRumors. There aren’t any specific details about what changes iOS 28 will introduce for notifications. “The sources said iOS 28 will include significant changes to Notification Center, but we do not have any specific details,” the report says.

The iOS notifications system is overdue for an update. While Apple has added features like Apple Intelligence-based priority notifications and notification summaries, the system still lacks other organization and sorting settings.

Android 16 introduced several significant notification changes, focused primarily on reducing clutter and prioritizing important information. For Pixel devices, the update also introduced Notification Organizer, a feature that automatically groups and silences low-priority alerts, including promotions, news, and social media notifications.

As Abner explained on 9to5Google last year:

The Notification Organizer will sort your alerts into the following categories: Promotions, News, Social, and Suggested. The first two are already on, but you must enable the remaining ones. There’s also an option to “Always expand bundles.”

I’d love for Apple to adopt a similar system on iPhone, iPad, and Mac. Even with the recent Apple Intelligence additions, the iOS notifications system is still far too basic.

What changes do you think Apple should make to notifications with iOS 28? Do you use features like priority notifications and notification summaries? Let us know down in the comments.
