The iPhone 17e is newer, and a lot better value

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Black Friday is upon us, and there's no shortage of discounted smartphone deals available for you to take advantage of right now. However, one Black Friday phone deal you should probably avoid is the iPhone 16e. For some reason the ageing e-series iPhone is trending, despite the fact that the iPhone 17e is available — and much better value for money.

I was a little confused about why people would be hunting for iPhone 16e deals, seeing as how it's coming up to its second birthday. So I went looking to see if there were any deals that might have knocked the phone down to an enticing price. Sadly I had very little success.

There's always been demand for older iPhones, and I've come across people trying to convince me that the positively ancient iPhone 5c is gaining traction with the youth of today. I don't buy that, but I'll admit that I haven't looked into it. Anyway...

The fact that flagship iPhones are so expensive and hold their value compared to similarly-priced Androids means that people gravitate towards older models due to the lower price tag. Phones like the iPhone 16e, which started life as a relatively cheap option have the capacity to drop even further, which bolsters their long-term popularity.

Which I totally understand. The downside is that unused iPhones don't stick around for more than a couple of years, and the iPhone 16e is in that situation right now. When I went hunting for deals, the majority of listings I found were for used or refurbished handsets. I don't have anything against used phones, but they're not the kind of thing a lot of people would expect when Black Friday rolls around.

The only brand new deal I could find was at Walmart, with an iPhone 16e that's locked to Walmart's Straight Talk carrier — an MVNO powered by Verizon. While the phone is $200, I'm not sure that it's the right deal for most people.

Grab the iPhone 16e at Walmart for just $199. The only caveat is that this phone is locked to the retailer's Straight Talk MVNO. Still you get a nice display, A18 performance, a solid solo camera and access to Apple Intelligence.

For starters, picking up a Walmart iPhone 16e means you are locked into Straight Talk for at least a year. The carrier's unlock policy mimics that of Verizon, and it means you have to have owned your phone for at least 365 days before it can be unlocked.

By which point the iPhone 18e will have been released, and the iPhone 19e likely only be months away. This means that the iPhone 16e will be borderline obsolete by next November.

On top of that, I actually found some deals for the iPhone 17e that are a lot cheaper. While the difference between the phones isn't enormous, the upgrades Apple afforded to the 17e make it a much more enticing handset — including MagSafe and improved performance from the A19 chipset. However, these deals do come with some caveats of their own.

Get your iPhone 17e for just $0.43 a month at AT&T, no trade-in required. All you need to do is sign up for an eligible 36-month plan and Apple's cheapest handset can be yours for less than $16.

As you can see, AT&T is offering the iPhone 17e for $0.43 a month over a 36 month contract. That means the total you'd pay for the phone itself is $15.48. That's pretty incredible for a phone that was released back in February.

Meanwhile a model with 512GB of storage is $6.43 a month, which works out to a total cost of $231.48. It's not the same kind of discount, but it's still a hefty price cut.

AT&TB isn't the only carrier with deals either, since T-Mobile is offering a free iPhone 17e.

Apple iPhone 17e: was $699 now free w/ T-Mix plan @ T-Mobile

Grab a free iPhone 17e at T-Mobile, so long as you sign up for a 36-month T-Mix plan and meet the other eligibility criteria. That includes signing up for a new line and porting your old number, or trading in an old device first.

The downside here is that you need to meet a bunch of T-Mobile's criteria. The first is to sign up to a T-Mix plan with at least one monthly "Pick" perk while porting your number from another carrier and opening a new line. Alternatively a new line and trade-in is an option, but you need to add an extra Pick to your plan — and pay the additional cost.

Still, free is free, and that's a lot less than $15.48. Though the caveat is both devices will be locked into that specific plan for another three years — at which point the iPhone 20e could be on the way.

While I'm well aware that the jump from iPhone 16e to iPhone 17e wasn't that big, I'm personally more inclined to pick the 17e. Not only because the deals cost less money upfront, but also because the addition of MagSafe is a huge benefit. I'm a big fan of MagSafe's accessory support, and that makes the 17e a much more useful phone.

That said, the iPhone 17e deals are locking you into three year plans, which may not be something you want to do. Especially when the alternative is being locked into Straight Talk for a year.

In the end, the right decision is the one that you make for yourself.

#3227. Judge orders Apple to produce 3,200 documents in Epic Games dispute

A federal judge has ordered Apple to produce a random sample of 3,200 documents for Epic Games to review, following Epic’s allegations that Apple improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

With Apple and Epic trading arguments in the Supreme Court over whether the civil contempt ruling against Apple should stand, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

In August, Apple submitted its proposal to the district court, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%. Epic, however, is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

Earlier this month, Epic accused Apple of improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching a set of search terms agreed upon by both companies to help identify documents that could shed light on how Apple arrived at those rates.

[…] Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple says decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s new CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness.

Apple, in turn, pushed back against Epic’s accusations, saying the search terms were overly broad and had captured large numbers of documents unrelated to the proceedings.

[…] at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms […]. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

The company also asked the court to reject Epic’s motion to order it to produce all non-privileged documents matching the agreed-upon search terms, and alternatively suggested submitting a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deemed nonresponsive to a Special Master for independent review.

As it turns out, neither company got exactly what it originally wanted, but the judge ruled largely in Epic’s favor on how to determine whether Apple had improperly withheld documents.

Following a hearing in which both companies presented their respective proposals for how a randomized sampling of the documents should be conducted, Magistrate Judge Thomas S. Hixson decided to adopt Epic’s proposal, which called for Apple to produce a random sample of 3,200 documents it had previously deemed nonresponsive, along with their associated document families, for Epic itself to review.

All documents in the sample will be drawn from the files of the seven Apple custodians referenced in Epic’s original motion.

Apple, by contrast, had suggested a considerably smaller sample of 383 documents, arguing that this would be statistically significant at a 95% confidence level.

In his decision, Judge Hixson agreed that Epic had legitimate reasons to question Apple’s reasons for withholding the documents:

Apple’s responsiveness rate is so dramatically low that it raises red flags. With Apple screening out more than 99% of the documents that hit on the agreed search terms, it is unreasonable to ask Epic to believe that Apple is making these responsiveness calls in good faith. That is particularly true in this case, in which Judge Gonzalez Rogers has sanctioned Apple for its large-scale abuse of the attorney-client privilege for the purpose of obscuring the evidence.

Judge Hixson also rejected Apple’s suggestion that a Special Master conduct the review, arguing that given the level of familiarity with the case required to assess the relevance of these documents, Epic was the only practical option for determining whether Apple had systematically misclassified them.

Realistically, the only person who has the practical ability to determine if Apple has been systematically mis-coding documents as nonresponsive is its opponent, Epic.

In his decision, the judge agreed with Apple that the company should be allowed to review the documents for privileged and sensitive information before producing them to Epic, and authorized Apple to designate all documents produced as part of the exercise as Attorneys’ Eyes Only.

Importantly, Judge Hixson has not yet determined whether Apple systematically misclassified responsive documents as nonresponsive, nor has he imposed the daily monetary sanctions originally requested by Epic.

Apple now has until December 8 to complete the document production, with Epic having until December 15 to file any objections, and Apple until December 22 to respond.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Amazon's Black Friday 2026 sale has brought the Sonos Arc Ultra down to $849 from its usual $1,099, a $250 discount that marks its lowest price yet. PCMag named it the best soundbar of 2024 and gave it an “outstanding” rating in its review. Still, $849 is a lot to spend on a single soundbar, and anyone shopping on a tighter budget will find more affordable picks in our Fire TV soundbar roundup. For more editor-vetted tech deals, check out our comprehensive Black Friday coverage.

For those who can make room in their budget, the next thing to plan around is space, since the Arc Ultra measures a little over 46 inches across and weighs about 13 pounds, making it a natural match for a larger TV. Despite all that width, it keeps a low profile at just under three inches tall, so it can sit beneath most screens without blocking the picture, or you can wall-mount it if you would rather keep your TV stand clear. All that size makes room for a 9.1.4-channel layout (a big step up from the original Arc) that gives Dolby Atmos effects more space to spread around and above you. Sonos also added a new Sound Motion driver that it says doubles the original Arc's bass, giving action scenes real weight without a separate subwoofer, though you can still add a Sub 4 later for more rumble.

At the other end of the sound spectrum, voices and dialogue come through clearly even at low volumes, and a Speech Enhancement mode lifts them further. Trueplay tuning then adjusts the sound to your room, with a quick version on Android and iOS and a more detailed one for iPhone owners. The biggest drawback is connectivity, since the Arc Ultra has a single HDMI eARC port with no passthrough, which can leave you short on inputs for a console or streaming box, and no optical port. It also lacks DTS:X support, a letdown for some Blu-ray collectors, and voice control is limited to Alexa or Sonos' own assistant, though Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and AirPlay 2 make streaming music from your phone easy.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

#3223. Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab CEO on How He Reached the C-Suite

Anthony Vetro’s journey from multimedia pioneer to executive

Kathy Pretz is the editor in chief of The Institute, IEEE's member publication

At the 2025 IEEE Vision, Innovation, and Challenges Summit, IEEE Fellow Anthony Vetro discusses the need for open innovation models to keep pace with rapid technological change taking place at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories.

The trajectory from researcher to top executive at a leading R&D organization doesn’t happen overnight. It took Anthony Vetro nearly 30 years to climb the corporate ladder at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass. He joined MERL in 1996, right out of college, and he has worked there ever since.

Vetro probably is best known for his research in multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.

Anthony Vetro Employer Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass.Title President and CEO Member grade FellowAlma mater Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school)

Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass.

Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school)

He became an IEEE Fellow in 2011 for his contributions to video coding, three-dimensional television, and multimedia adaptation.

Mitsubishi Electric has moved away from making televisions. It now focuses on developing systems including ones used for defense, electronics, the energy industry, and space exploration.

His ascension up the executive ranks began in 2018, when he was named a vice president and director of MERL. In 2023 he was appointed its president and CEO.

He also works closely with the company’s new U.S.-based innovation facility in Cambridge. And he recently took on a dual role as deputy head of Mitsubishi Electric’s global R&D activities, including in Asia and Europe.

Vetro credits IEEE with helping him develop his management skills after he served in several IEEE Signal Processing Society leadership positions. He also learned from his key roles in establishing international standards for digital image formats and video compression, he says.

“Between my IEEE activities, standards work, and some of the business shifts in Mitsubishi Electric, I eventually graduated to more management leadership roles,” he says.

Vetro is the son of immigrants. His father came to the United States from Italy and his mother from Sweden when they were both in their early 20s. They settled in New York City, on Staten Island.

Although neither parent went to college, his father stressed the importance of education to his son at an early age.

“My father started in the mailroom and worked his way up to eventually managing communication accounts and infrastructure for large financial companies,” he says. “My mother worked in banks, first as a teller and later doing bank reconciliation after pursuing some professional certifications.

“Through their jobs, they saw people with college degrees getting better positions and promotions, so education was something really ingrained in me.”

Vetro says he developed a passion for mathematics and engineering in middle school. He was accepted into the Staten Island Technical High School, a specialized pre-engineering institution. There he solidified his interest in pursuing a career in the field.

“A lot of students didn’t know what they wanted to major in at college, but I knew fairly early,” he says.

He was accepted into the accelerated bachelor’s and master’s engineering degree programs at the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school). He began his bachelor’s degree program in 1992 and the master’s program in 1994.

“As part of the master’s degree program, I needed to do a thesis,” he says. “I wasn’t sure exactly what it would be on. Soon after taking my first course on image processing, I was certain that was an area I wanted to work in.”

It was an interesting time, he says, because broadcast television was going through a major transformation, shifting from analog to digital during the early 1990s. It was long before streaming services, he notes.

“I feel that industry-level engagement in IEEE is very vital to the organization in maintaining high relevance in the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity.”

“The idea of being able to come up with compact ways to represent this very rich information was really appealing to me,” he says. “I’m also a visual learner. I liked seeing images, and there was some nice math behind them, too.”

After he earned both degrees in 1996, Mitsubishi Electric hired him for its technical staff. He conducted research on multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.

“The opportunity to work on projects around digital TV broadcasting and image processing attracted me,” he says.

He conducted research in video conferencing, Internet and mobile streaming, and video coding technology, widely used for broadcasting, DVDs, and Blu-ray discs. He developed several technologies including digital TV receivers and displays, surveillance and camera-monitoring systems, automotive equipment, and satellite imaging systems.

Another advantage of joining the company, he says, was that it allowed him to pursue a doctorate in electrical engineering, also from Polytechnic, while working.

“That really sealed the deal,” he says. He received the degree in 2001.

After six years as a technical staff member, he was promoted in 2007 to manage the group working on digital video coding, processing, and streaming. Seven years later, Vetro became its deputy director, a top-level management position that he held until 2018.

“After working for about 10 years exclusively on video compression processing technology, there were some shifts in our company’s business. Its overall strategy began to change,” he says, “so I became interested in broadening my experience beyond video.”

He was asked to lead the lab’s speech and audio team. It was more development-oriented, he says, and focused on vehicle infotainment and speech interfaces before Alexa and Siri existed. He pivoted the team’s focus more toward research and established strategic paths tailored to emerging opportunities within the organization. Recognizing emerging trends in sensing and information security, he formed groups that worked on them.

To help spur innovation between Mitsubishi Electric and its U.S. customers, the company in June opened Serendie Street Boston, its first digital transformation hub in the United States. It’s colocated with MERL.

The new office is modeled after the first Serendie Street collaboration space, which Mitsubishi Electric launched in 2024 in Yokohama, Japan.

The word serendie is a combination of serendipity and digital engineering, according to the company’s website. Serendie is the digital platform designed to foster collaborations between data, people, and technology, it says. The space where people interact to extract ideas from the data is called “the street.”

The platform brings together researchers, startups, customers, and partners to identify new products, test them, run pilot programs, and scale them up.

Vetro says he’s excited about the endeavor.

“Serendie Street [Boston] aims to strengthen the bridge between our global R&D efforts and real-world industry challenges. The hub is intended to bring our partners and customers together to engage in more cocreation activities, where we listen to their problems and work together to solve them,” he says. “I think the company has come to recognize that we can’t just do it all internally by ourselves.”

The technologies being worked on include robotics, energy solutions such as integrating renewable energy into the grid, and more energy-efficient data center systems.

The decision to colocate the hub with MERL offices was deliberate, Vetro says.

“The area has a very rich ecosystem,” he says. “We have Harvard, MIT, and many other universities a stone’s throw away.”

Vetro joined IEEE in 1992 as a student member during an event the Polytechnic’s student branch was holding. He enjoyed reading the IEEE Potentials student member publication and other periodicals, he says.

“In the earliest stages of my career, IEEE was a place where I could attend conferences, read journals, and stay on top of the latest research and trends,” he says. “Over the years, I was able to build a professional network, which has been helpful. That facilitated a lot of research collaboration with university professors attending the conferences.

“In more recent years, IEEE has provided a great platform for industry to exhibit thought leadership and discuss real-world problems we’re facing. I think these discussions may have even set some research directions among the academic community.”

Vetro is an active volunteer for the IEEE Signal Processing Society. He has chaired several of its technical committees and conferences, and he served as an associate editor for some of its journals.

He says he’s most proud of establishing the society’s industry board and serving as its inaugural chair. The board formed a corporate engagement program, launched the Industry Signals newsletter, developed short courses tailored to industry, and holds career fairs at the society’s flagship conferences.

Vetro also had a hand in MERL sponsoring two IEEE technical field awards: the Flanagan Speech and Audio Processing Award and the Fourier Award for Signal Processing.

“Industry-level engagement in IEEE is really very vital to the organization in maintaining its relevance to the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity,” he says.

Kathy Pretz is editor in chief for The Institute, which covers all aspects of IEEE, its members, and the technology they're involved in. She has a bachelor's degree in applied communication from Rider University, in Lawrenceville, N.J., and holds a master's degree in corporate and public communication from Monmouth University, in West Long Branch, N.J.

#3221. Readdle’s Documents app adds voice recording with transcripts, summaries, more

Readdle updated its Documents app for iPhone and iPad this week with Voice Notes, a new AI-powered feature that lets users record conversations and automatically generate transcripts, summaries, and follow-up notes. Here are the details.

While the habit of recording meetings, lectures, or even one’s own thoughts is not particularly new, modern AI tools and models have made it considerably easier to extract useful information from these recordings without having to listen back to them in their entirety or take copious notes that can distract from the actual conversation.

This week, Readdle’s Documents introduced Voice Notes, which “lets you record audio and turn it into a summary, follow-ups, and a full transcript,” as the company put it.

Users can start a new recording session by tapping the “+” button in the app and selecting Voice Notes. Alternatively, they can start recording from the iPhone’s Action button, which is a nice touch.

Once they’re done, Readdle says Documents can generate:

Users can cycle through these three tabs, where they can also listen to the original recording or copy and share the information.

Readdle says Voice Notes can recognize multiple languages in the same conversation, with the actual transcript preserving the languages as spoken, “while the summary and follow-ups are generated in the most frequently spoken language.”

Each voice note is saved as a single file in Documents that contains the original recording, transcript, summary, and follow-ups. Users can organize these files into folders, share them, sync them with their cloud storage, and save the transcript as a separate .txt file.

However, if users give a voice note’s AI-generated content a thumbs down, Readdle may retain its transcript and summary for up to six months, or until the user objects to their processing, whichever comes first.

The company also says user data isn’t used to train AI models, although third-party AI providers may retain inputs for up to 30 days for abuse and misuse monitoring, or longer if required by law.

Chinese director Zou Jing’s A Girl Unknown won the top $75,000 Best Narrative prize at the Doha Film Festival as the second edition of its revamped format came to a close on Friday evening.

The China-set first feature follows the fate of a young girl who is found abandoned as a baby in a rubbish bin and then grows up from babyhood through to adolescence with three sets of different guardians and circumstances.

#3218. Report: Apple accounted for 57% of US smartphone shipments in Q3

Apple’s share of US smartphone shipments jumped from 50% to 57% year over year last quarter, with the company being the only major smartphone maker to buck the broader trend of declining shipments. Here are the details.

Yesterday, we covered a Counterpoint Research report on Q3 Latin American smartphone shipments, which showed Apple recording the smallest year-over-year decline among the region’s top five smartphone makers. As a result, Apple increased its share of regional shipments from 7% to 9%.

The report echoed the findings of several others published throughout this year, which showed how Apple has managed to navigate component shortages and rising costs better than many of its competitors, some of which have had to raise smartphone prices multiple times.

Apple, by contrast, kept iPhone pricing largely stable for much of the year, holding off on broader price increases until the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro lineup in September.

Today, Counterpoint Research released its report on US smartphone shipments for Q3, which showed that Apple increased its share from 50% to 57% year over year, amid a 9% decline in overall shipments.

According to a separate Counterpoint report published last Thursday, Apple was the only major smartphone maker to avoid a year-over-year decline in shipment volume during the quarter.

In today’s report, Counterpoint notes that rising memory costs hit the low-end Android segment particularly hard during the quarter. Samsung was the only major Android smartphone maker to increase its shipment share, seeing a one-percentage-point bump to 25%, “helped by a portfolio spanning flagships and the low-end Galaxy A-series.”

Carriers also felt the impact of the broader downturn, with smartphone sales across the three major US carriers collectively falling 4% year over year, per the report.

Looking ahead, Counterpoint expects memory costs to remain elevated and US carriers to be more selective with their holiday promotions, with smartphone sales expected to remain weak in Q4 despite it typically being the strongest quarter of the year.

#3216. How Engineers Designed a Mission to One of Jupiter’s Icy Moons

The Europa Clipper will probe below the frozen surface for possible habitats for life

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum.

Tim Larson is the project manager for NASA's Europa Clipper, which is on its way to study Jupiter's icy moon in the 2030s.

On 3 December 2026, a 30.5-meter-wide space probe will slingshot past Earth, picking up the speed it needs to reach Jupiter in 2030. The Europa Clipper is designed to investigate Jupiter’s enigmatic moon Europa and look for places that could support life in the ocean beneath the moon’s thick shell of ice. Tim Larson is the project manager for the mission at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, and he spoke to IEEE Spectrum about designing and flying the Europa Clipper.

Tim Larson Tim Larson is the project manager for NASA’s Europa Clipper mission. He has been at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., for over 35 years.

Tim Larson is the project manager for NASA’s Europa Clipper mission. He has been at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., for over 35 years.

Why take such a roundabout route to Jupiter?

Tim Larson: That’s all driven by the energy that we got from our launch vehicle, the Falcon Heavy. It set a MEGA trajectory: Mars-Earth Gravity Assist. So about 4 months after launch, we flew by Mars, got an assist there. Now we’re coming back in for a final assist from Earth to get on our outbound trajectory to Jupiter.

The Europa Clipper is set to orbit Jupiter and fly by Europa about 50 times to study it. Why not just orbit it directly?

Larson: The big challenge is the radiation environment. It is so intense that any spacecraft orbiting Europa wouldn’t last very long. So the mission designers came through with this concept of the flybys.

We will be in a three-week orbit around Jupiter, but the orbit is synchronized so that every time we fly by Jupiter, Europa is right there. Over time, you build up the coverage of the surface that we’re ultimately after. We spend a relatively short time in the high-radiation environment, and then the rest of the orbit is in a more benign environment where we can relay data back down to Earth, et cetera.

The Europa Clipper relies on solar panels to generate power. Why not use a compact radioisotope thermoelectric generator (RTG)?

Larson: It’s a national policy to only use RTGs if it is absolutely essential. A lot of the early concepts that focused on orbiting Europa had to go with RTG approaches, because you’d spend so much time in the shadow of Jupiter. Once we shifted over to the flyby mission approach, it turned out solar arrays would be feasible.

How are Europa Clipper’s electronics different from other probes?

Larson: One of the things that we dealt with in our design was the level of radiation tolerance that we had to get in all our parts. In our main avionics module—we call it the vault—everything in there is designed to an exposure of 150 kilorads (1,500 sieverts). To get our usual factor-of-two margin, we were buying parts that rated to 300 kilorads.

That brings up side challenges, because when you buy high-radiation-tolerance versions of parts, you can’t always get the exact same part functionality. You might have to change your circuits a little bit. And they don’t always have the same form factor, so you have to accommodate that.

How do you preserve fine-grained technical knowledge about the spacecraft over its yearslong mission lifetime?

Larson: By the time we launch, we try to get everything documented. As we learn about the idiosyncrasies of the spacecraft, we capture that in databases. When we have personnel turnover, we try to have a lot of overlap. We’re looking at how AI can take in this broad array of information we have in multiple different formats and locations, and extract information.

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “Tim Larson.”

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum. He currently helms Spectrum's Hands On column, and is also responsible for interactive projects such as the Top Programming Languages app. He has a bachelor's degree in experimental physics from Trinity College Dublin.

South Korea’s Fair Trade Commission (KFTC) announced today that it has opened formal proceedings against Apple over its advertising of Apple Intelligence features for the iPhone 16 lineup. Here are the details.

Back in March 2025, shortly after Apple announced it was delaying the rollout of what would eventually become Siri AI, the South Korean civic group Seoul YMCA filed a complaint with the KFTC.

At the time, Yonhap reported that the organization had previously called on Apple to compensate affected customers, and alleged that the company may have continued to market the iPhone 16 lineup despite already knowing that some of its advertised AI features would be delayed.

As 9to5Mac readers will likely remember, Apple widely advertised Apple Intelligence and AI-powered Siri features as part of its iPhone 16 launch campaign, going so far as to give its iconic Fifth Avenue store an Apple Intelligence-themed makeover and run an ad campaign starring Bella Ramsey.

This landed Apple in legal and regulatory trouble in multiple markets, including the US, where the company agreed to a $250 million class action settlement earlier this year, and Brazil, where it came under scrutiny from a consumer protection agency in May. Now, the company is facing potential penalties in South Korea as well.

As a result of Seoul YMCA’s complaint, the KFTC conducted an investigation into Apple’s advertising practices. Today, the regulator announced (via MacRumors) that its investigators had submitted their findings and recommendations for formal deliberation by the Commission.

According to the KFTC’s press release, investigators concluded that Apple advertised Apple Intelligence and its planned staggered rollout on the iPhone 16 website, but “concealed, downplayed, or omitted information material to consumers’ purchasing decisions.”

That included, per the press release (translation ours):

The press release also notes that Genmoji, Image Playground, “Siri with the ability to understand personal context,” and “Siri that provides step-by-step guidance” were not made available as advertised:

For example, Siri’s ability to understand personal context was advertised as being scheduled to launch first in US English by the end of 2024, as currently available in US English in October 2024, and as scheduled to support Korean in early April 2025.

In reality, the feature was not launched in US English until September 2026, with Korean language support following in October 2026.

As a result, the investigators concluded that Apple’s conduct constituted a violation of the country’s Labeling and Advertising Act, which prohibits deceptive labeling and advertising.

They recommended issuing corrective orders, including a prohibition on such conduct in the future, as well as imposing a financial penalty.

They also estimate that Apple’s revenue associated with the alleged violation amounts to approximately 3.35 trillion South Korean won (roughly $2.5 billion), though the KFTC’s press release does not specify the amount of the fine.

⁠Yonhap noted today that the fine could reach roughly $48 million, while ⁠KBS reported that it could range between $21 million and $42 million.

With the report now submitted, Apple has six weeks to submit its written defense before the Commission deliberates and makes a final determination on whether the company violated the law and, if so, how much it should be fined.

Update, November 27, 12:08 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said:

At Apple, we deeply value the relationship with our customers in Korea and have always focused on delivering the best products and services in the world. Since we added Korean language support for Apple Intelligence last year, users have benefited from dozens of powerful features that are integrated across Apple’s platforms. And we have continued to build on that commitment with the recent launch of Korean language support for Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri that’s more capable, conversational, and personal. We have cooperated with the KFTC’s investigation and disagree with the conclusions in the Examiner’s Report. We look forward to presenting a fulsome defense before the Commission.

#3214. David Byrne On Getting Into Character As Elon Musk For ‘Musk’ Song “Let Me Sell You A Dream” – Crew Call Podcast

On today’s Crew Call we chat with near EGOT winner David Byrne about “Let Me Sell You A Dream,” his new song for Alex Gibney’s controversial documentary Musk about, yes, Elon Musk.

Byrne tells us about co-writing the ditty during the European leg of his latest tour “Who is the Sky?” and biking to a London musical equipment shop to get recording gear, so he could create a makeshift studio in his hotel room and lay down tracks for Oscar nominated composer Daniel Pemberton, who is a co-writer on the song.

In recording the tune, Byrne exclaims, “I’d sit at my little mic stand in a hotel room and I’d go into character as Elon Musk (exhale), and just start ranting.” Related Stories News 'American Psycho' Gets Axed: Luca Guadagnino Confirms His Adaptation Is "Not Happening" News 'Artificial' Filmmaker Luca Guadagnino On Whether AI Is Humanity's Doomsday & Sam Altman's Arsenal - Crew Call Podcast

Off the bat, “Let Me Sell You a Dream” in its fast dance tempo brings to mind the 1986 Talking Heads single “Wild Wild Life” which Byrne wrote for the Warner Bros absurdist reality movie he directed and co-wrote, True Stories. Watch on Deadline

Byrne says that “Let Me Sell You a Dream” had to be “hard hitting…It’s going to have an impact at the at the end. It has to jump right in, and grab you by the throat.”

“It’s not one of those fading-while-the-credits roll and everybody decides, ‘I’m going to get up, get out and get back to my car before everybody else.'”

“Let Me Sell You a Dream” is also throwback to the types of pseudo anti-yuppie tunes that Talking Heads was known for including 1988’s “(Nothing) But Flowers” and 1979’s “Life During Wartime”. Byrne explains that the Musk end-credits song was arguably the “fastest” he has ever written in his career. To date, while Musk has railed against Gibney about the documentary, he hasn’t sent any praise or tomatoes to the Oscar winning Byrne. Give a listen to Byrne’s process here:

Byrne also takes us down memory regaling that his first instrument was a violin, and how he grew up inspired by The Rolling Stones and Motown. He also chats about the early days of the Talking Heads when they were discovered by Sire Records’ boss Seymour Stein (“He could meet with us, talk with us and and sing ours songs back to us”) as well as working with Bernardo Bertolucci and producer Jeremy Thomas on the score for The Last Emperor which won Byrne an original score Oscar which he co-shared with Cong Su and Ryūichi Sakamoto.

A time when Byrne was told by the music industry he was too audacious? How about when he did his first solo album in 1989, the Latino infused “Rei Momo”?

“They implied that I shot myself in the foot and that the fans were going to leave,” said Byrne, which if you look at the full houses for his concerts, not to mention the Broadway run of his concert show American Utopia is definitely not the case: His appearance last November at the Dolby Theater drew the likes of Oliver Stone, Judd Apatow and Derek Waters, while his Hollywood Bowl late August appearances for “Who Is The Sky?” were jam packed.

“I thought that if I keep trying different things, you’re not going to get pigeonholed as being the blues rock band or the funk band,” Byrne shares, “I thought if I can do different things, that’s going to give you wiggle room, and allow you to do different things down the road and hopefully the audience goes with you.”

And of course, we ask the never-ending question to Byrne, that even after a great reunion with the Talking Heads for the A24 Imax 2023 re-release of seminal concert film Stop Making Sense, will they ever tour together again?

#3211. Justin Timberlake Visits Jimmy Fallon And Shares Thanksgiving Dish On New Apple TV Doc Series, How David Bowie Influenced ‘SexyBack’ & Performs Dance Classics

Thursday was a dual celebration for Justin Timberlake‘s visit with Jimmy Fallon on NBC’s Tonight Show: There was Thanksgiving, of course, which you can see in the photo above was most certainly not ignored by the two old friends, and then for the former boy bander the visit was an opportunity to celebrate the 20th anniversary of his album FutureSex/LoveSounds.

And of course there’s always new material to plug, and last night it was Timberlake‘s four-part doc series streaming on Apple TV beginning December 11.

The Thanksgiving visit began with Timberlake joining Fallon in a musical number celebrating “The History of Party Songs.” With Timberlake initially putting up some mock reluctance, the two then launched into Soul II Soul’s “Back to Life (However Do You Want Me),” then proceeded through a smorgasbord of classic dance hits, including Ini Kamoze’s “Here Comes the Hotstepper,” Mark Morrison’s “Return of the Mack,” Montell Jordan’s “This Is How We Do It,” Spice Girls “Wannabe,” Bell Biv DeVoe’s “Poison,” Timberlake’s own “Rock Your Body,” Wild Cherry’s “Play That Funky Music White Boy,” “Good Times” by Chic, Cool and the Gang’s “Celebration,” and some others you might be able catch before the big finish of The Backstreet Boys’ “I Want It That Way.” Related Stories News Ariana Grande Crashes Jimmy Fallon's Monologue With 'Focker-In-Law's Ben Stiller & Robert De Niro Late Night TV 'Tonight Show': Jimmy Fallon & Jamie Lee Curtis Channel Fielder & Holmes In Cold Open

Watch the musical medley here: Watch on Deadline

Timberlake also reflected on the making of the FutureSex/LoveSounds album, noting that at the time of its recording he’d been listening to “Bowie, David Byrne, Talking Heads, Freddie Mercury, Queen, Billy Idol, James Brown, Eurythmics, INXS…but we were kind of thinking, How we can take the sonics of dance music and flip it?”

Timberlake recalls that, as presented in the upcoming docuseries, his record label at the time was not initially impressed with the album, thinking it was “too fast,” to which Timberlake responded, “That’s why it’s going to work.” He also remembered that the label was disappointed that he wasn’t using his signature falsetto enough. “I was listening to [David Bowie’s] ‘Rebel Rebel’ a lot…and that music at that time sounded so daring.” Timberlake says he wanted to create the impression that the singer was a character in the song, as Bowie so often did, and the result was “SexyBack.”

Regarding the upcoming four-part Timberlake documentary series, the singer explained that he overcame his initial reluctance – “I’m sort of famously private” – by trusting director and friend Fisher Stevens. “I feel like I’ve gone through a lot in the last five years that made me a better human,” he said.

“But the more we sat down and talked, the more I found myself searching for something that was beneath the surface a little more,” he continued. “And I think that at the end of the day I sort of mustered up some courage to talk about things that I’ve never talked about before. Things that even those that are closest to me don’t know.”

Timberlake also paid tribute to the late singer-songwriter D’Angelo, the major influence who died October 14, 2025. “D’Angelo, for me, he changed everything,” Timberlake told Fallon. “You know, he was one of those artists. Rest in peace. What a brilliant, brilliant, brilliant artist. But I remember when he came out, it just like everything changed. [He] was a once-in-a-generation artist.”

And finally, here’s Timberlake’s performance that capped the Fallon appearance, taking place at New York’s famed Rainbow Room atop 30 Rock. He performs a medley of “FutureSex/LoveSound,” “SexyBack,” “Summer Love” and “My Love.”

The docuseries Timberlake airs on Apple TV on Friday, December 11 with the first two episodes, followed by the third episode on Friday, December 18 and the finale on Wednesday, December 23, 2026.

#3209. ‘The Hunting Wives’ Pays Tribute To Lionsgate Exec Salli Newman

Viewers of the second season of The Hunting Wives, currently streaming on Netflix, will find a poignant message at the end of the season finale: “In Loving Memory of Salli Newman.”

Newman was the senior vice president of television production at Lionsgate, producer of The Hunting Wives. She died of a heart attack on December 8, 2025, in her Burbank home at the age of 67, according to her family.

Hunting Wives showrunner Rebecca Cutter told Entertainment Weekly that Newman died during the filming of Season 2. “So we dedicated the final episode to her,” Cutter said. “And, yeah, that was really sad. She was such a hard worker. She so loved the show, and it was just really devastating.” Related Stories News Netflix Posts Racy Thanksgiving Message On 'The Hunting Wives' Season 2 Premiere Day News Netflix's 'The Hunting Wives' Season 2 Trailer Promises "Someone Is Going Down"

Newman was also included in the 2026 Primetime Emmy Awards In Memoriam broadcast on September 24. Watch on Deadline

Newman moved to Los Angeles after graduating from Montana State University and launched her show business career at 19, training as an actor and stuntwoman while working as a secretary/assistant at Consolidated Film Industries.

“Salli soaked up all the knowledge she could from industry veterans,” her family notes, “and worked hard to learn her craft. She created Firebrand Productions in 1990 and spent the next 30 years as an independent producer, working on both made-for-tv movies and feature films, plus several series for both networks and streaming services.”

Among her many producing, co-producing or executive producing credits were D2: The Mighty Ducks (1994), When a Man Loves a Woman (1994), Naomi & Wynonna: Love Can Build A Bridge (1995), Bunheads (2013) and 31 episodes of Greenleaf (2018-2020).

In 2020, Newman was hired as a Senior VP of Television Production at LionsGate Films in Santa Monica, where she worked until her death in December 2025.

Newman is survived by four sisters, two brothers, stepmother Joan Newman, five step-siblings and numerous nieces and nephews.

The second season of The Hunting Wives, starring Malin Akerman, Dermot Mulroney and Brittany Snow, is available to stream on Netflix.

#3208. This ER Doctor Became a Hospital’s First Clinical AI Engineer

Dinesh Rai’s role as Boston Children’s prompt engineer quickly outgrew its bounds

Jackie Snow is a Los Angeles-based freelance journalist.

In his home office, Dinesh Rai splits his time between working with engineers and clinicians at Boston Children’s Hospital.

When Boston Children’s Hospital posted a job listing for a prompt engineer in 2023, Dinesh Rai decided to apply. He didn’t expect to get the job.

At the time, prompt engineering was being touted as one of the hot new jobs created by generative AI. Companies wanted people who knew how to coax the best answers from large language models (LLMs) by carefully wording instructions, supplying examples, and giving the systems personas or other context.

Dinesh Rai Employer: Boston Children’s HospitalOccupation: Clinical AI EngineerEducation: Bachelor’s degree in supply-chain management and marketing sciences, Rutgers Business School; Doctor of Medicine, Albert Einstein College of Medicine

Bachelor’s degree in supply-chain management and marketing sciences, Rutgers Business School; Doctor of Medicine, Albert Einstein College of Medicine

It was an unusual role for a hospital, but Rai had an unusual résumé. While he was trained as an emergency physician, he had also taught himself to code just before entering medical school. After completing a fellowship in clinical informatics—which focuses on the intersection of clinical practice and IT systems—he moved into health technology.

Boston Children’s brought him on board in August 2023. Three years later, Rai still works there. Prompt engineering, however, has become a much less important part of the job.

When he joined, the expectation was that prompting would become a job in itself. “Knowing how to prompt AI properly was going to be the job function of the future,” says John Brownstein, chief innovation officer at Boston Children’s.

Early on, the hospital needed internal expertise about how to begin using AI, Brownstein says. Now, better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems—and determining whether its answers can be trusted. Brownstein says the questions they focus on these days have shifted: “How do you embed these tools in your day-to-day operations? How do you build agents to manage literally everything that you do?”

For Rai, that has meant embracing a job broader than the role that brought him to Boston. “I’m more like a clinical AI engineer now,” he says.

Rai originally studied business as an undergraduate and began teaching himself to code in 2014 (the same year he entered medical school), as neural networks and image recognition were starting to attract wider attention. He kept building software while training as a doctor. In medical school, for instance, he created a platform called Academius for students to track residency interviews and assemble their rank lists.

For Rai, the appeal of coding was its scale. In emergency medicine, he could make a direct difference for the individual patient in front of him. Software offered the possibility of building something that thousands of clinicians might use for many more patients.

His 2021–22 informatics fellowship made the possibility of doing that full-time feel real. In 2022, Rai took a job at Pieces, a health care AI company, where he led work to bring LLM-based medical summarization into clinical use.

That meant taking a break from practicing medicine altogether. “Stepping away was definitely a hard decision,” Rai says. But he wanted to give the technology work his full attention. He has since reactivated his medical license and hopes to return to clinical practice in some capacity within the next year.

At Boston Children’s, roughly half his day now looks like an engineer’s: working with developers, writing code, and advancing projects from the technical side. The other half is spent with clinicians, figuring out what they actually need. That combination has become the point of the job.

One project, called clinical doppelgangers, is designed to help doctors treating complicated patients find similar cases buried in the hospital’s historical data. Medical guidelines are generally based on large populations, but at a hospital that handles rare and complex diseases, an individual child may not fit neatly into the populations represented in published studies.

The system is being developed to let clinicians identify previous patients with relevant similarities, examine their trajectories, and see how different interventions turned out. It is not meant to replace randomized clinical trials. Instead, it could provide another source of evidence when a physician is facing a case for which the published literature offers little guidance.

Projects like that require more than knowing how to ask an LLM the right question. They require understanding what hospital data means, how a clinician will use an answer, and how an AI system can go wrong.

Rai recently encountered some of those challenges while working on another project with a clinical team and a development team. They were deciding how much of a patient’s medical record to give an AI model when asking it to identify findings relevant to a particular clinical outcome.

Better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems.

Both groups initially favored giving the model access to more information, but for different reasons. The developers assumed any data point could be useful. The clinicians assumed the model would recognize irrelevant findings and ignore them.

Rai saw a problem with both assumptions. Clinically, an abnormal lab result or vital sign is not necessarily relevant to the question being asked. And from a technical perspective, an LLM cannot be counted on to recognize that irrelevance. If the system asks the model whether a given abnormality matters, it may construct a plausible explanation for why it does, even when the record does not support the connection.

“That’s where the dual perspective has been valuable,” Rai says, “not just translating between teams, but recognizing when an approach that looks reasonable from either perspective rests on assumptions we shouldn’t make.”

In medicine, the challenges surrounding the prompt are now more important than polishing the prompt itself. Is the model’s output consistent with the underlying data? How should its results be evaluated? Will the clinician using it be able to recognize a mistake?

That also means listening to clinicians’ experience. For the platform Rai’s team built to draft clinical notes, the clinicians who would go on to use the tool reviewed a batch of generated notes before anything was finalized. Someone who had cared for a complicated patient in the cardiac intensive care unit for weeks would catch an error far more easily than someone skimming the chart afterward, Rai says.

Although AI adoption in medicine is surging, some health care professionals still have concerns about its use. “I think some skepticism is healthy, and we don’t try to talk people out of it,” he says. The team told clinicians up front that it was a generative AI tool meant to support their judgment, not replace their own review of the chart. “People trust it more when they’ve seen its mistakes than when we just tell them it’s good.”

The evolution of Rai’s role reflects how quickly AI-focused jobs can change, so Rai is wary of telling people interested in careers like his to master any particular tool. For people who want hands-on engineering jobs, fundamental programming skills still matter. Some understanding of machine learning is useful, as is experience building and testing systems. But not every clinician who wants to work with AI needs to become a database architect or take a deep dive into algorithms.

What Rai considers indispensable is domain knowledge. In the medical field, that means understanding how health care workflows operate, how electronic health record data is created, what that data actually represents, and where care breaks down.

That may be the more durable lesson from a career that briefly carried one of AI’s buzziest job titles.

“The value isn’t just knowing how to get an answer from a model,” Rai says. “It’s knowing what context it needs and whether that context supports the answer we’re asking it to give.”

Jackie Snow is a Los Angeles-based freelance journalist focusing on technology.

#3207. These M5 MacBook Air Laptops Are up to $300 Off During Black Friday

Apple announced a slew of products in March, including the MacBook Air with the M5 chip, which ended up increasing in price in June due to the RAM shortage. These MacBooks come in both 13-inch and 15-inch sizes, and if you're interested in either, it's a good time to buy: In the lead-up to Black Friday, Amazon is selling both at up to $300 off.

Those discounts bring the 13-inch MacBook Air to $1,034.10 (down from $1,299) and $1,299.99 (originally $1,499.99) for the 512GB and 1 TB versions, respectively. The 15-inch MacBook Air is down to $1,199 (originally $1,499), and the 1TB version is $1,549.99 (originally $1,799.99). All versions are at their lowest prices since the June price hikes.

The M5 MacBook Air is the best laptop for most people looking for a new machine in 2026. In comparison to the already excellent M4 Airs, the M5 base model has double the storage at 512GB. The powerful M5 chip makes the performance even smoother, according to Mashable's review. The aluminum design is as good as you'd expect from Apple's most popular portable laptop, lightweight and thin. It comes with a Liquid Retina display, Touch ID, a 12MP Center Stage Camera, and the Magic Keyboard.

Typically, the question would be whether to go for the slightly older M4 MacBook Air or pay a bit more for the newer M5 chip—but given how tough it is to find a new M4 laptop used, and the fact that most refurbished ones are the same price as the M5 with 512GB of storage, it makes the choice to go with the M5 a no-brainer—especially with a $250 discount.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3201. Belgium’s Wallonia halts Google data centre after permit was revoked

Google kept building after Wallonia revoked its permit to cool servers with Sambre river water. Greenpeace raised the alarm, and the case goes to court in January.

Google’s data centre campus in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium

The Walloon Region has ordered Google to stop building its data centre near Charleroi in Belgium. Work had carried on for months at the site in Farciennes and Aiseau-Presles without a valid permit. The order came on Thursday, days after Greenpeace Belgium asked the regional government to step in.

About 300 construction workers were on the site when the order came, Walloon official Raphael Stokis told Belgian broadcaster VRT. The Walloon infrastructure minister, François Desquesnes, had announced an investigation on Wednesday.

Google’s original permit, granted in 2024, covered three data centres cooled by air. In 2025 the company changed its plans. It merged two of the buildings into one larger building and switched to cooling with water from the Sambre river, Greenpeace said.

The Walloon administration approved that amended permit in April 2026. After residents appealed, Desquesnes revoked it in August. The request covered 600 cubic metres of river water an hour, the minister said. Less than a quarter of it would have gone back into the river, according to Belga.

Residents then told Greenpeace that work was still going on. The group investigated, using satellite images, and launched an emergency procedure earlier this week.

“Tech giants are not above the law,” said Nadia Cornejo, a Greenpeace Belgium spokesperson. “This should already have been the case in August, when the permit was cancelled.”

Google appealed the revocation but did not wait for the court to rule before carrying on with the work, VRT reported.

Google is committed to “an open and collaborative dialogue with the regional government and experts” on its investments in Wallonia, a spokesperson told VRT.

On 17 October it asked Belgium’s Council of State to annul and suspend the minister’s decision. Greenpeace and several residents asked to join the case on 16 November, and a public hearing is set for 7 January.

Data centres have faced similar local opposition elsewhere. Google’s Finnish data centre project drew a police investigation, and residents in Indonesia’s Batam protested over water in October. In the US, voters rejected data centre measures at the midterms.

The Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 robot vacuum and mop is down to $799.99 from $1,299.99 in an early Black Friday deal, saving you $500 and bringing it to its lowest price to date. Much of its appeal comes from a slim 3.1-inch profile that lets it reach under beds, sofas, and other low furniture where taller robot vacuums often can’t fit. It manages this with a feature Roborock calls RetractSense, which checks the clearance as the robot approaches a tight gap and lowers the laser navigation tower into the body, leaving a camera with a 100-degree field of view to guide it underneath.

Beyond its low profile, the Qrevo Edge 2 pairs 25,000Pa of suction with a split DuoDivide main brush that guides hair toward the suction opening, so long strands and pet fur are less likely to end up wound around the roller. Edges get extra attention too, since its FlexiArm Arc side brush reaches out into corners while its mop module swivels to get closer to walls, with the two mop pads spinning at 200 RPM as they work. It also adjusts its cleaning based on whether it encounters dry or wet dirt, boosting suction for dust and lifting its main brush over spills. For all that adaptability on the floor, getting between rooms can be trickier—the robot lacks an adjustable chassis to lift itself over obstacles, so it can struggle with thresholds higher than 0.8 inches.

Once a cleaning run wraps up, most of the upkeep happens at the dock, which washes and dries the mop pads and empties dust into a bag rated for up to 65 days. That said, its onboard water tank is relatively small at 2.3 fluid ounces, potentially requiring extra trips to the dock during larger mopping jobs. There's also no dedicated cleaning solution tank, meaning you'll have to add approved cleaning additives manually to the fresh water. The rest of the fine-tuning happens in the Roborock app, where you can set cleaning schedules, adjust suction power and water flow, and choose how the robot handles carpets.

The Work and Pensions Secretary calls it a serious cyber incident. Downing Street has not ruled out an attack, and benefit payments continue as normal.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden called it a “serious cyber incident”, and Downing Street said there is currently no evidence of customer data loss. Some claimants told the BBC their payments had not arrived. TNW has updated this article.

The UK’s Department for Work and Pensions has taken its online services offline after detecting a cyber incident. The department, which runs Universal Credit, the state pension and most other British benefits, confirmed the incident on Friday morning.

“We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems,” the department said in its statement.

The department says the incident does not affect regular benefit and pension payments, which will arrive as normal. People who need help can call their usual benefit line.

The systems for pensions, Universal Credit and Personal Independence Payment applications are down, the BBC reported. So are Tell Us Once, which people use to report a death, and state pension applications.

McFadden said the department was aware of an issue on Thursday and “did the right thing” by taking services down to protect people’s personal details. He said there was no evidence that the incident had compromised anyone’s data.

“When we get an incident like this, the most important thing to do is to protect the public,” McFadden said, according to the BBC.

The Prime Minister’s official spokesperson called it a “live and ongoing incident”. Officials could not rule out that a malicious actor was behind it.

“Currently there is no evidence of customer data loss. But the investigation is ongoing so I’m not going to get ahead of that process,” the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson added there was no evidence that a malicious actor had targeted other government departments. DWP is working with the National Cyber Security Centre, part of GCHQ, and the Government Cyber Coordination Centre.

Some Universal Credit claimants told the BBC they had not received their payments on Friday. DWP said the incident had not affected regular payments. It asked anyone with problems to call its benefit phone line.

Debbie Abrahams, who chairs the Work and Pensions Committee, said taking systems offline was “absolutely the right thing”. Chi Onwurah, chair of the Science and Technology Committee, said the disruption “should be a wake up call”.

“Quite often we are working on extremely old computer systems,” DWP’s permanent secretary, Sarah Healey, told MPs on 4 November.

In 2025-26, DWP spent £309.5bn on benefits and pensions for about 23 million people, its annual report says.

DWP is the second major institution in two days to take systems offline over a cyber incident. News agency AFP took its content platform offline on Thursday. In the US, a FinCEN hack took Treasury systems offline this week, and Switzerland reported AI agent cyberattacks on critical infrastructure.

Whether you're ready to dive headfirst into the Christmas spirit or craving something heavier, this weekend's lineup has you covered. Based on the second of the Heartbreaker Bay novels by Jill Shalvis, this Christmastime romance centers on San Francisco pet shop owner Willa Davis (Rachel Melvin), who, a decade after Keane Winters (Thomas Beaudoin) stood her up in high school, re-encounters the fella who slighted her when he comes into her shop in need of a cat sitter for the holidays.

Though Willa still harbors a grudge, she unexpectedly falls for Keane — even though he doesn't remember hurting her all those years ago. Directed by Ashley Avis, the 2017 film also stars Flo Lawrence, Alexandra Weaver, and Annie Thurman.

Watch "The Trouble with Mistletoe" on Netflix now

You already know Victor Hugo's "The Hunchback of Notre-Dame," but while that classic French tale is famously set in 15th-century Paris, this Netflix adaptation moves up the action to 1830 on the eve of the July Revolution, around when Hugo himself published his most famous work.

As political turmoil and cholera threaten to ravage the City of Light, a hunchbacked stonemason named Quasimodo (played by César winner Vincent Cassel), believed to resist the disease, is hunted down by police for medical experiments. Things get even more complicated when Quasimodo falls for a dancer named Agnès (Daphné Patakia), an unrequited love that leads the hunchback to risk everything to keep her safe.

#3194. iOS 27.3 adds limits for these advanced features, details here

iOS 27.3 launches soon with a key change: certain advanced AI features will have daily usage limits. In an article posted on X, leaker pdfu details how this new system works.

When iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and iPadOS 27.3 arrive next month, Apple will implement usage limits for advanced AI features.

Some Apple Intelligence capabilities will continue having unlimited use—mainly ones that run locally. But for server-based features that use Private Cloud Compute (PCC), users will have daily allowances on a per-device basis.

Apple has shared some official word on how usage limits work, but many of the finer details haven’t been publicized yet. However, leaker pdfu has discovered a lot about the behind-the-scenes rules governing usage limits. Many were shared this week in an article posted on X.

For example, here’s each feature’s “standard device limit” in daily tokens per pdfu:

As explained in pdfu’s article, token usage depends on the complexity of requests. He writes:

Not all features make the same number of requests. Generating one image in Image Playground, or a single query to the AFM 3 Cloud model in Shortcuts, consumes one token. Siri AI requests may make multiple connections to PCC, as server models make tool calls and receive results. Here’s a timeline of how the query “Find a bookshop near me that’s open right now” uses 2 Siri tokens:

It’s also worth noting that not all Siri AI requests will use tokens—only “advanced” requests. If you’re interested in reading more, pdfu also recently outlined what counts as an “advanced” Siri request, which you can read here.

Do you expect these usage limits in iOS 27.3 to be a problem for you? Let us know in the comments.

Meredith's beloved Forerunner 970, the top-of-the-line Garmin for serious runners, is $649.99 right now, down from an original price of $749.99.

My pick would be the Garmin Forerunner 265 for $299.99. It's a slightly older model, but still works well and is packed with features for runners.

#3192. Huawei founder Ren Zhengfei tells NYT to pass his thanks to Trump

Ren Zhengfei, 82, told the paper in October that China will eventually overtake the US in chips. Huawei still makes less than 4% of Nvidia’s AI computing power, Epoch AI estimates.

US sanctions pushed Huawei and China into self-reliance, and Huawei’s founder, Ren Zhengfei, wants Donald Trump thanked for it. Ren spoke to Keith Bradsher and Adam Satariano of The New York Times at Huawei’s Shenzhen headquarters in October. The paper published the interview on Thursday.

“Pass on our thanks to him, and also share the story of the Trump Corridor as well,” Ren told the Times.

Huawei executives call a gilded hallway at the headquarters the Trump Corridor. It is named after the president whose first-term campaign tried to cut Huawei off from advanced chips and global telecoms networks. After the crackdown, Ren said, Huawei became “a company of our own country”. He is 82 and still Huawei’s chief executive.

The interview ran two days after a federal jury in New York convicted Huawei. The jury found it guilty of conspiring to steal trade secrets from US companies and of bank fraud linked to Iran. Huawei said the verdicts were “without legal or factual merit”.

It also came as the US tightened its curbs on Nvidia’s chips. On 16 November the US moved to restrict remote access to American AI chips through overseas data centres. Huawei’s Ascend processors have become China’s leading alternative to Nvidia’s chips, the Times reported.

Huawei now spends more than $27bn a year on research and development, according to the Times. It has worked with Chinese AI companies, including DeepSeek, to adapt their models to its chips. It argues it can rival Nvidia by linking many processors into one large system, even if each chip is weaker.

The gap remains wide. Huawei will make less than 4% as much AI computing power as Nvidia this year, research firm Epoch AI estimates. Its most powerful chip, the Ascend 950, delivers about half the performance of Nvidia’s H100, which began shipping in 2022.

China also still lacks the most advanced chipmaking equipment, including lithography machines from the Dutch company ASML. Huawei has been working to fill other gaps at home, including its own AI memory.

Many in Trump’s first administration believed the restrictions could destroy Huawei, the Times reported.

“We thought this could be a death blow,” Liza Tobin, then a China policy official at the National Security Council, told the Times.

Ren, speaking before Nvidia’s recent leadership turmoil, said China would eventually overtake the US in chips. “It’s just a matter of time,” he said. He said he still hoped the two countries could repair their relationship.

“We have now established a complete chain that allows us to survive,” Ren told the Times.

Sony's XM6 are the latest flagships. They weigh very little and sound excellent — and now you can get them for $100 off. As you'll see in our Sony WH-1000XM6 review, they offer excellent noise cancellation, improved call quality over prior models, and an epic 30 hours of battery life. Flagship quality, and now mid-range price.

Sheer elegance and class. That's how I'd describe the Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3. I actually own and use a set of these on a near daily basis at home. The Px7 S3 have a warmer, bassier tune than the reference-y Px8 S2 (also on sale), but you still get that Bowers refinement and fidelity.

Another flagship drop! The AirPods Max 2 drop have dropped a little lower before now to $399, but not by much. And given these are the latest flagships from Apple no less, $130 is a surprisingly good chunk of cash off.

As well as the Px7 S3, I also own the Px8 S2. So I'm pretty well place to dispense some sage advice here: buy the Px8 S2. No, seriously, you won't regret it. I know, I know: they're pricey, but they make up for it in spades with beautiful, spacious, high fidelity sound, plus exquisite build quality and strong ANC.

#3189. Shoppers ask AI for Black Friday deals, but few let the bots pay

Black Friday is the biggest test yet for AI shopping agents. Amazon is blocking Meta’s Muse, and only 23% of US shoppers trust AI to pay for them.

Traffic from AI services to US retail sites more than doubled on Thanksgiving from last year, Adobe told the Associated Press. Shoppers spent a record $7.1bn online that day, up 10.4%. Adobe expects $12.9bn on Black Friday itself.

Purchases made by AI agents are a far smaller slice. They made up 0.4% of global e-commerce transactions and 0.2% of their value, according to Bain & Co research. Annie Palmer reported the figures for CNBC.

This weekend is the biggest test yet for the shopping agents from Meta, Google, OpenAI and Amazon. Each wants to help people find gifts and, in time, buy them. The early evidence points to three problems. Shoppers do not trust the bots with their money. Many retailers will not let them in. And nobody agrees who pays when an agent gets it wrong.

A Morning Consult poll for Visa found that 54% of adults have used AI for at least one shopping task, up from 47% last year. Only 23% trust generative AI to make payments for them, Phil Wahba reported for Fortune.

The price of the item matters too. In an American Express survey, 52% of US consumers were happy for an agent to buy cheap items such as groceries. Only 15% felt the same about electronics and appliances, the big sellers of Black Friday.

That caution has some basis. Visa sent 22 AI models on 15 shopping tasks earlier this month, and they failed 42.8% of their runs. In more than half of the failed runs, the agent still bought something.

British shoppers are trying the tools too. Meta launched Muse in the UK this week, with partners including Marks & Spencer, Sainsbury’s, JD Sports and Currys. A third of people planning to shop in the sales intend to use AI, up from 19% last year, according to a YouGov poll. Almost half of the shoppers who use AI worry about biased or sponsored results, Sarah Butler reported in The Guardian.

Even shoppers who want an agent to buy for them may find it cannot. About half of big retailers and popular brands do not let AI assistants shop their sites. London software firm Human Forward found this after testing ChatGPT, Gemini, Muse and other agents on 200 websites, Spencer Soper reported for Bloomberg.

Amazon has gone furthest. It blocked Muse from its store in September. It is also suing Perplexity over the shopping agent in its Comet browser, in a case due for trial next year. Amazon is reportedly in talks with Meta about Muse, but the block is still in place.

“Agentic third-party applications such as Muse have the same obligations, and we’ve requested that Meta remove Amazon from the experience,” an Amazon spokesperson told Bloomberg.

Amazon’s advertising business is expected to bring in $81.9bn this year, Bloomberg reported. Bots that browse for shoppers could undercut it. Chief executive Andy Jassy told investors in October that outside agents were not meaningfully hurting its ads business.

“The natural question is whether agentic shopping from external horizontal agents is meaningfully impacting Amazon ads, and the answer is no,” Jassy said on Amazon’s earnings call.

Other companies limit agents rather than ban them. eBay, United Airlines and Kohl’s restrict what agents can do or block them, CNBC reported. Some retailers let bots browse but stop them at the checkout. Agents that do get in can still get stuck at logins and CAPTCHA tests.

Maia Bittner, chief product officer at fintech startup Imprint, told CNBC she asked Muse to buy windscreen wipers from AutoZone. Seventeen hours later, the agent said AutoZone had cancelled the order over an error. Its suggestion was to buy them on Amazon herself.

The bigger question for retailers is liability. Some have written their answer into their terms of service. Best Buy treats an agent’s purchases as if the customer had made them.

“Best Buy is not responsible for conduct, errors, actions, or inaction by any Digital Agent,” the company’s terms state.

Card and payment companies are taking on some of that risk. American Express has said it will protect eligible customers from charges caused by an agent’s errors. Stripe, whose Link wallet works with Muse, offers a refund guarantee on some agent purchases. JPMorgan Chase went the other way last month and blocked outside agents from acting for its customers, citing security, CNBC reported.

In the UK, TrueLayer is testing another route. Its pilot lets an agent pay by bank at Papa John’s, under the FCA’s watch.

“In Europe especially, retailers are asking a simple question: if the bot gets it wrong, who’s liable?” Mark Howell, director of European retail at e-commerce firm Rithum, told The Guardian.

Meta says that in the UK, Muse must ask for approval before it buys anything. A separate “security agent” checks its actions against the permissions a user has granted.

The tech companies are pressing on. Muse reached 10 million users in the US and Canada about six weeks after its September launch, Bloomberg reported. Mark Zuckerberg told investors in October that shopping was its most common use, with users spending $200 on average. He expects Meta to take a small fee from transactions. Google has launched Universal Cart, which puts items from several retailers in one basket.

McKinsey estimates agentic commerce could generate $1tn of US economic activity by 2030. Retailers, meanwhile, are bracing for more AI-driven cyberattacks around the sales.

Matt Kochmann, a tech executive, tried ChatGPT, Muse and Claude to find a case for his new iPhone. None of them stood out, he told Bloomberg.

“It just doesn’t feel magical yet,” he said.
